person: Nikita Khrushchev, First Secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union
card: The Kremlin and Novo-Ogaryovo. From the deployment decision in May to the broadcast of 28 October · 16 decisions. How to bring back the missiles you sent to Cuba, or whether to bring them back at all.
intro: You are Nikita Sergeyevich Khrushchev, 68, First Secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and Chairman of the Council of Ministers. In May 1962 you decided to deploy medium-range missiles in Cuba in secret, and over the next five months 70–80 ships crossed the Caribbean. Beside you sits the Presidium. Mikoyan is cautious, Kozlov is rough, Gromyko arrives with the Foreign Ministry’s drafts, and Malinovsky, the defense minister, says little and begins with the numbers of his orders. Your aide Troyanovsky handles the telephone and the cables. Ambassador Dobrynin in Washington and Ambassador Alekseev in Havana report the mood in the room by coded cable. In Cuba, Pliyev, commander of the Group of Forces, goes by the code name “Pavlov,” and the defense minister by “Trostnik.”
allyLabel: Trust of Cuba and the Socialist Camp

NK-00.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, Presidium meeting room
NK-00.title: The Hedgehog

map.caption: Havana lies about 170 kilometers from Key West, and the shortest distance from Cuba’s north coast to Florida is about 150 kilometers (90 miles). At Guantánamo, on Cuba’s eastern tip, the United States keeps a naval base.

telegram.from: Marshal Malinovsky, defense minister; Marshal Zakharov, chief of the General Staff
telegram.to: N. S. Khrushchev, First Secretary, Central Committee of the CPSU
telegram.subject: On the deployment of Soviet forces on the territory of Cuba
telegram.text: Three R-12 regiments (24 missiles) and two R-14 regiments (16). 1.5 missiles and warheads per launcher, total 60 missiles, 60 warheads. / Two FKR cruise missile regiments (16 launchers, 5 special warheads per launcher). One Il-28 torpedo-bomber regiment. Two air defense divisions (24 S-75 battalions, 576 missiles). Sopka coastal missiles. 12 motor torpedo boats. / Four ground regiments. Total strength about 44,000. 70–80 transport ships. / Code name “Anadyr.”

NK-00.event: Three days ago, on 21 May, you raised the matter of aid to Cuba in the Presidium. The proposal was to come to terms with Castro, conclude a joint defense treaty, deploy nuclear missiles, carry it out in secret and announce it afterward. Two days of debate followed, and today Malinovsky and Zakharov have come back with the figures.
NK-00.scene: Malinovsky’s memorandum lies on the long table of the meeting room. The plan is to carry 40 missiles, 60 warheads and 44,000 men across the Atlantic in 70–80 ships. You were in Bulgaria until last week, and you came home thinking of the American Jupiter missiles going into Turkey across the Black Sea. At the Bay of Pigs in April the Americans failed once; the second time, you believe, they will send their own army. On the back of the memorandum General Ivanov of the General Staff’s Main Operations Directorate has written a note: the Anadyr measures are approved unanimously and in full, on condition that Castro agrees, and a delegation including Marshal Biryuzov and Rashidov will go to Cuba to obtain his consent. At the end of the table Mikoyan is polishing his glasses; Kozlov leafs through the memorandum, nodding.

voices.who: Nikita Khrushchev (your words on 21 May, as recorded in the Malin notes)
voices.text: Come to an agreement with Fidel Castro. Conclude a military treaty on joint defense. Deploy nuclear missiles there. Do it secretly. Then announce it. The missiles stay under Soviet command. This will be an offensive policy.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: Nikita Sergeyevich, whether Castro will accept, and whether 40 missiles can be stood up under the palm trees out of sight of American reconnaissance planes, someone has to go and see first. If they are found, the Americans will read it as a declaration of war.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: The figures are done. Deployment can be completed by the end of October. Camouflage is feasible. For the commander, a ground forces general will attract less notice than a rocket forces man.

choices.text: Sign and announce the defense treaty first, as Castro wants, and bring in the missiles openly under a published treaty
choices.why: With a treaty the deployment is legal and nothing to hide
choices.after: Gromyko read the draft treaty to the Presidium on 1 July, and Raúl Castro came to Moscow in July. But the announcement was put off again, because Malinovsky kept saying that the moment it was published the Americans would stop the shipping. The ships began to sail in secret.

choices.text: Adopt Malinovsky’s plan: deploy in secret and announce in November, but first send a commission, making Castro’s consent the condition
choices.why: The only way is a fait accompli before the Americans know
choices.after: The Presidium approved your proposal and adopted the plan. Biryuzov and Rashidov went to Havana under the name “Engineer Petrov,” and Castro accepted on the spot. On 10 June you said, “We are moving toward deciding the matter. I think we will win this operation,” and on 6 July Pliyev was named commander.

choices.text: Defer the decision, as Mikoyan’s doubts suggest. Let the Biryuzov commission check on the ground whether the launch sites can be hidden, and ask again in June
choices.why: A missile that cannot be hidden is a target, not a shield
choices.after: The commission came back in early June and reported that deployment was feasible. Biryuzov said the palm trees would hide the missiles, and you made the decision on 10 June. Two weeks were lost, but the plan went down the same road.

note.text: The 24 May memorandum is published in English translation in the Wilson Center Digital Archive (113038); the document number does not appear in the published text. Ivanov’s note on the back (113045) shows that approval was conditional on Castro’s consent. That in late June you told Pliyev’s deputy commanders you had decided to “slip a hedgehog in on the Americans” rests on General Garbuz’s 1992 recollection. Mikoyan’s objection in May is a secondary account, based on the memoir of his son Sergo Mikoyan.
note.src: WC/UMD 113038; WC/UMD 113045; Malin 5/21; Malin 6/10; Garbuz 1992

pressure.title: The Hedgehog and the Bay of Pigs
pressure.text: You came back from Bulgaria with the American missiles in Turkey fixed in your mind. In your memoirs you later said the idea of a Cuban deployment came to you on that trip. After the American failure at the Bay of Pigs a year ago, you believed the next invasion would bring American troops themselves, and you later wrote in your memoirs that you feared the Soviet word would carry less weight in the socialist camp if Cuba fell. On 21 May you yourself told the Presidium this would be an offensive policy, and all that survives is the fact that two days of debate followed. That Mikoyan raised doubts is a story handed down through his son, and when General Dementyev heard what you told the deputy commanders in late June, he answered that a secret deployment was impossible. Even so, on 10 June you said you thought you would win this operation.
pressure.src: Malin 5/21; Malin 6/10; WC/UMD 113038; WC/UMD 113045; Garbuz 1992; WC/UMD 91043; Khrushchev Remembers 1970

NK-01.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, papers for signature
NK-01.title: The Lunas and a Draft

telegram.from: Marshal Malinovsky, defense minister; Marshal Zakharov, chief of the General Staff
telegram.to: N. S. Khrushchev, First Secretary, Central Committee of the CPSU
telegram.subject: On reinforcing the Group of Soviet Forces in Cuba
telegram.text: Add one Il-28 squadron (6 aircraft, 6 407N nuclear bombs). / Add three “Luna” battalions (6 launchers, 12 special warheads, 24 conventional rounds). / Enclosure: draft instruction to the commander of Soviet forces in Cuba. In substance: should the enemy land and contact with the Defense Ministry be lost, the commander may on his own decision employ the nuclear means of the Lunas, Il-28s and FKR-1s. Single copy drafted 8 September by Major General Yeliseyev; read 10 September by Lieutenant General Davidkov.
telegram.sign: R. Malinovsky / M. Zakharov (enclosed draft instruction unsigned)

NK-01.event: On 4 September the White House confirmed that Cuba held surface-to-air missiles, missile boats and 3,500 technicians, said there was no evidence of offensive capability, and warned that if there were, the gravest issues would arise. On 11 September TASS issued a statement that the Soviet Union had no need to move its weapons beyond its borders. Congress is taking up a resolution on Cuba, and the U.S. Navy is preparing landing exercises in the Caribbean.
NK-01.scene: Back from your holiday, you find Malinovsky’s second memorandum on your desk. The strategic missiles are still at sea, and you cannot shake the thought that the Americans may land before the deployment is complete. Hence the proposal: send more short-range tactical nuclear weapons to strike a landing force on the beaches. An enclosure is attached. It is the draft of an instruction that would let the commander use nuclear weapons on his own if contact with Moscow were lost. Malinovsky prefers to pass such things by word of mouth rather than put them on paper. Troyanovsky, turning the pages, stops at the enclosure. A delegation left on paper is a responsibility left on paper.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: Once a landing begins, communications between Havana and Moscow may be cut for hours. If Pliyev waits for Moscow then, the Lunas will hit an empty beach instead of the landing force. But I do not put such things in writing. Passing it on orally is enough.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: Authority given by word of mouth is remembered by no one once war comes. Give Pliyev a signed document. Then he can fire, and the Americans, knowing it, will stop.

voices.who: Oleg Troyanovsky (aide)
voices.text: Nikita Sergeyevich, if that document ever comes to light it will be read as the Soviet Union handing the key to nuclear war to a general in the field. Sending the weapons and letting him use them are two different decisions.

choices.text: Send the Lunas and the Il-28s, but pass the conditions for their use only through Malinovsky’s oral instructions. Do not sign the written delegation in the enclosure
choices.why: A compromise: keep the nuclear key in Moscow but leave the field some latitude
choices.after: The draft remained a single unsigned copy. The same day General Staff directive No. 76438 brought forward the deadline for the missile division’s combat readiness, and on 25 September it was decided that each boat of the submarine brigade would carry one nuclear torpedo. The surface squadron that was to bring the cruisers never received its sailing order.

choices.text: Sign the enclosed draft. If a landing and a break in communications coincide, let Pliyev decide for himself on the nuclear use of the Lunas, Il-28s and FKRs
choices.why: Missing the landing force while waiting for Moscow is the greater danger
choices.after: The signed instruction went into Pliyev’s safe. Malinovsky went on adding orally that “nothing without Moscow’s permission,” but the document remained a document. No one then knew what it would come to mean in October.

choices.text: Along with the Lunas and Il-28s, send the surface squadron with its two cruisers as planned. Nuclear use only on orders from Moscow
choices.why: A Soviet flag visible at sea makes both blockade and landing harder
choices.after: The order to prepare the surface squadron for sea went down to the Northern Fleet. But cruisers are ships that cannot be hidden, and U.S. Navy patrol aircraft began counting them off the coast of Norway. The most conspicuous ships of all had been added to a secret operation.

note.text: The 8 September memorandum and the enclosed draft are scanned in the National Security Archive collection (620908), and an English translation is on page 183 of Gribkov and Smith, Operation Anadyr. According to Savranskaya’s annotation the draft was a single handwritten copy and Malinovsky did not sign it. Whether Pliyev held advance authority over the tactical nuclear weapons is the first issue in the Phase 1 report; the majority view is that no valid delegation existed on paper. The surface squadron including two cruisers (Mikhail Kutuzov and Sverdlov) was in the 24 May memorandum, and according to the Northern Fleet report the sailing order was never given. That you decided on the additional tactical weapons at your Pitsunda holiday residence on 7 September is not in the Malin notes and rests on secondary sources only.
note.src: NSA CMC 620908; Phase 1 issue 1; NSA 2022 doc 2; WC/UMD 113038; Northern Fleet report 1962-12

map.caption: The ships of Operation Anadyr came in mainly through the ports of Mariel and Havana, and the R-12 regiments were deployed in the west and center of the island.

NK-02.time: Morning (night of the 18th in Washington and Havana)
NK-02.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, the First Secretary’s office
NK-02.title: Completely Satisfactory

telegram.subject: Conversation with President Kennedy (18 October, 5 p.m., White House)
telegram.text: Everything we know about the U.S. government’s position on the Cuban question allows us to conclude that the overall situation is completely satisfactory. / In the present circumstances a U.S. military adventure against Cuba is almost impossible to imagine. / Following the prepared text, I stated that Soviet assistance is exclusively defensive and that I wished to stress the word “defensive.” Kennedy reread his statement of 4 September.

NK-02.event: The Presidium meetings of 11 and 14 October had no Cuban item; the agenda was the border conflict between India and China. In Cuba, Sidorov’s R-12 regiment will reach combat readiness on 20 October, with the other two regiments to follow. The two R-14 regiments and the Aleksandrovsk, carrying the warheads, are still at sea.
NK-02.scene: Gromyko’s cable came in overnight and lies on your desk this morning. Kennedy received Gromyko in the Oval Office for more than two hours and said not a word about the missiles in Cuba. Gromyko writes that the situation is completely satisfactory. You intend to announce the treaty and the missiles together once the American midterm elections are over in November. Three weeks remain, and the Americans are reported not to know. Troyanovsky cannot take his eyes off the line about Kennedy rereading his 4 September statement. That statement said the gravest issues would arise if offensive weapons were present. Malinovsky has brought in the shipping schedule.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister, cable)
voices.text: Everything we know about the U.S. government’s position on the Cuban question allows us to conclude that the overall situation is completely satisfactory. In the present circumstances a U.S. military adventure against Cuba is almost impossible to imagine.

voices.who: Oleg Troyanovsky (aide)
voices.text: Why would Kennedy reread his 4 September statement? A man who knows nothing does not bring out an old statement. I read it as Comrade Gromyko being tested in that room.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: One R-12 regiment is ready tomorrow and the rest within ten days. The R-14s come in early November. Hurry, and the camouflage suffers. If the Americans do not know, as reported, the schedule should stand.

choices.text: Accept Gromyko’s report and leave the schedule as it is. Announce the treaty and the missiles together in November, after the American midterms
choices.why: Trust the report that the Americans do not know, and complete the fait accompli
choices.after: The next day Gromyko met Rusk again and reported Rusk as saying that “Cuba without the Soviets is one problem, but Cuba run by Soviet personnel is another.” You later remarked that Gromyko had answered Rusk mostly from an ethical standpoint. Three nights later, Dobrynin’s cable arrived.

choices.text: Announce the defense treaty now, as Castro has demanded since the summer. Let the Soviet Union speak first, before the Americans discover anything
choices.why: Saying it yourself hurts less than being caught
choices.after: Gromyko began drafting the announcement of the treaty. But before the text was finished, a cable came from Washington. Kennedy would speak on the evening of 22 October, and no time was left for the Soviet Union to speak first.

choices.text: Order Malinovsky to hurry the R-14 regiments and the Aleksandrovsk’s warhead shipment, and to recheck the camouflage at the launch sites
choices.why: Impatience: the better the reports, the more urgent it is to finish before discovery
choices.after: The order went out, but ships at sea could go no faster. Before the camouflage report came up, Dobrynin’s cable arrived first, on the night of 22 October. Kennedy would make a major speech that evening.

note.text: Kennedy had been looking at the U-2 photographs since 16 October and decided not to show them to Gromyko at the 18 October meeting (U.S. record, FRUS XI d29). Gromyko’s report is printed in CWIHP Bulletin 5, which gives no cable number. “Disclose the missiles to Kennedy” was never proposed on the Soviet side and is not offered as a choice.
note.src: Gromyko 10/19 (Bulletin 5); FRUS XI d29; Malin 10/22

NK-03.time: 10 p.m. (3 p.m. in Washington, 2 p.m. in Havana)
NK-03.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, Presidium meeting room
NK-03.title: Four Hours Before the Speech
NK-03.clock: Four hours until Kennedy’s speech (7 p.m. Washington, 2 a.m. on the 23rd in Moscow)

telegram.to: Pavlov (commander, Group of Soviet Forces in Cuba)
telegram.at: 22 October 1962, to be sent at 11:30 p.m.
telegram.subject: Raising combat readiness
telegram.text: In connection with a possible landing in Cuba by American forces now on maneuvers in the Caribbean, take urgent measures to raise combat readiness and to repel the enemy by the joint efforts of the Cuban army and all Soviet units. / Statsenko’s means and all of Beloborodov’s cargo are excluded.

NK-03.event: Dobrynin’s cable came in the afternoon. Kennedy will speak on radio and television at 7 p.m. Washington time on a “matter of the highest national urgency,” and it appears to concern Cuba. Alekseev in Havana reports that Cuba is calm. You have called the Presidium for 10 p.m.
NK-03.scene: Under the chandelier of the meeting room sit the Presidium members, Malinovsky and Gromyko. Malin takes notes in a corner. No one knows what Kennedy will say. Malinovsky has said he does not believe the Americans can mount a blitzkrieg right now and the speech will be a pre-election show. You have said you were not trying to start a war but to intimidate the Americans into keeping their hands off Cuba, and that you have been caught without having shipped everything you meant to ship and without having published the treaty. If the Americans attack, Soviet troops will fire back, and that could spread into a great war. On the table is the draft order to Pliyev that Malinovsky has brought: raise combat readiness and repel a landing force together with the Cuban army, but Statsenko’s R-12s and Beloborodov’s nuclear warheads are excluded. You have suggested that if there is an air assault the tactical nuclear weapons should be used, and Malinovsky has raised his hand.

voices.who: Nikita Khrushchev (your words, as recorded in the Malin notes)
voices.text: The point is that we were not going to unleash war. We wanted to intimidate the Americans into keeping their hands off Cuba. The difficulty is that we have not shipped everything we wanted to ship and have not published the treaty. The tragic thing is that they may attack, and we shall respond. This could turn into a big war.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: I do not think the United States could undertake a blitzkrieg operation at present. The radio speech is a pre-election show.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister, on your proposed tactical nuclear instruction)
voices.text: Wait until 1 a.m. Otherwise we give them grounds to use nuclear weapons.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: We must speak before the speech comes out. Announce on the radio that we have a treaty with Cuba and declare that all equipment in Cuba belongs to Cuba, and the pretext for an attack disappears.

choices.text: Authorize Pliyev to use tactical nuclear weapons. If there is an air assault, repel it with tactical nuclear weapons, but have the strategic means await orders from Moscow
choices.why: Fear that if the landing force is not hit on the beaches, every missile will be lost
choices.after: Malinovsky said no more, and the exclusion clause was struck from the draft. At 11:30 p.m. the order conditionally authorizing the use of tactical nuclear weapons went out in cipher. At 1 a.m. the text of the speech arrived. It was a blockade, not a landing.

choices.text: Take Malinovsky’s advice: put off the decision until the text of the speech arrives at 1 a.m., and send only the order raising combat readiness, with the nuclear means excluded
choices.why: Caution: nuclear weapons cannot be released before you know what the other side is doing
choices.after: No. 4/389 went out at 11:30 p.m. as drafted. Statsenko’s missiles and Beloborodov’s warheads were excluded. At 1 a.m. the text of the speech arrived. It was a blockade. There was no landing, and you spent the night in the meeting room. The Presidium meets again at 10 in the morning.

choices.text: Before the speech, announce the defense treaty with Cuba on the radio and declare that all equipment in Cuba is Cuban property, removing the pretext for an attack
choices.why: A propagandist’s calculation: whoever speaks first frames the story
choices.after: After midnight Radio Moscow announced the signing of the treaty. Two hours later Kennedy’s speech landed on top of it. It was a blockade. The American papers wrote that the Soviets had rushed out a treaty just before the speech, and the order raising combat readiness went out with the nuclear means excluded.

note.text: The Malin notes record you dictating an instruction: “if there is an air assault, the tactical nuclear weapons; the strategic means not until ordered.” But No. 4/389, sent at 11:30 p.m., expressly excluded the nuclear means. Malinovsky’s hold prevailed, and the Phase 1 report classed this as “proposed but not adopted.” The text of No. 4/389 is in Wilson Center 117316 and on page 363 of Gribkov’s Na krayu propasti.
note.src: Malin 10/22; WC/UMD 117316; Phase 1 issue 6

pressure.title: The Night You Were Caught
pressure.text: Tonight you must decide without knowing what the Americans will do. Malinovsky says the speech is a pre-election show, but you know you have not shipped everything you meant to ship and have not published the treaty. The R-14 regiments and the warheads for Cuba are still at sea, and you have said that if the Americans attack, Soviet troops will fire back and it could become a great war. In Hungary in 1956 you hesitated and then sent in the army; in Berlin in 1961 you ended it with a wall. This time the opponent is the United States, and when you proposed releasing the tactical nuclear weapons to Pliyev, Malinovsky raised his hand and asked you to wait until 1 a.m. His reason was that otherwise you would give the Americans grounds to use nuclear weapons.
pressure.src: Malin 10/22; WC/UMD 117316; Phase 1 issue 6; CWIHP 8/9 Malin 1956

NK-H9.time: 8 a.m. (1 a.m. on the 23rd in Washington, midnight in Havana)
NK-H9.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, Presidium meeting room
NK-H9.title: The Order That Went Out Before Dawn
NK-H9.clock: Two hours until the Presidium reconvenes (10 a.m.)
NK-H9.event: The text of the speech, arriving at 1 a.m., spoke of a naval quarantine, not a landing. The Americans would stop offensive weapons bound for Cuba, with the time of entry into force to be proclaimed separately. But your order of 11:30 p.m. allowed Pliyev to use tactical nuclear weapons if there was an air assault. In Havana it is decoded at 8 in the morning.
NK-H9.scene: The faces of the men who have sat in the meeting room all night are pale. Malinovsky finishes reading the speech and puts it down. A blockade is not a landing, but once American low-level reconnaissance begins, Cuban antiaircraft guns will fire, and if the Americans answer with bombing, Pliyev may use what he has been allowed. The order is already going into the safe in Havana. Mikoyan looks like a man who regrets having held his tongue last night. Kozlov says that changing the order will make Moscow look weak in Pliyev’s eyes.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: If it is a blockade, a landing is days away. In the meantime, if the Cubans bring down one low-flying aircraft and the Americans bomb a runway, Pliyev may read that as an air assault. Last night’s order must be corrected this morning.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: Nikita Sergeyevich, last night we thought a landing was coming. If it is not a landing, there is no reason to leave nuclear weapons in local hands. Send the amendment short, and give no reasons.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: Reverse an order overnight and Pliyev will wait half a day on the next one too. It takes less than a day for a blockade to turn into a landing.

choices.text: Keep the authorization. The moment a blockade turns into a landing, Pliyev will have no time to wait for Moscow
choices.why: Leaving the field commander empty-handed is the greater gamble
choices.after: The order stood. Pliyev acknowledged receipt, and guards were posted at the special-warhead storage of the Luna battalions and the Il-28 squadron. At the 10 o’clock meeting you moved on to the question of the ships.

choices.text: Correct the order this morning. Send an amending cable that expressly excludes the nuclear means, and respond to the blockade as the speech describes it
choices.why: If the other side has chosen a blockade, it is time to pull back the nuclear weapons
choices.after: The amending cable went out at 9 a.m. It was one line, excluding Statsenko’s means and all of Beloborodov’s cargo, and Pliyev acknowledged receipt before noon. The Presidium met again at 10 and took up the question of the ships.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact the nuclear means were excluded from the order of the night of 22 October, and No. 76639 of 27 October reaffirmed the prohibition. General Garbuz said in his 1992 recollection that he was told “use of the nuclear warheads of the FKRs, the Lunas and the aircraft without Moscow’s approval was forbidden.”
note.src: Phase 1 issue 1; Garbuz 1992; WC/UMD 117326

NK-04.time: 10 a.m. (3 a.m. in Washington, 2 a.m. in Havana)
NK-04.title: Half a Success

telegram.subject: President Kennedy’s radio and television address and meeting with Rusk
telegram.text: Kennedy made public “unmistakable evidence” obtained “within the past week” that Soviet medium-range missile bases are being built in Cuba. / Declared a naval “quarantine” on all offensive weapons bound for Cuba. Time of entry into force to be proclaimed later. / Requested meetings of the OAS and the Security Council. / Rusk summoned me an hour before the speech and handed over the text of the speech and the President’s letter to Comrade N. S. Khrushchev.

NK-04.event: Kennedy has chosen a blockade. Not a landing, not an air strike. But there are Soviet ships at sea: ships carrying missiles and warheads, ships passing through the Mediterranean, and, close to Cuba, the Aleksandrovsk with 24 R-14 warheads aboard. In the waters north of the Bahamas, four Northern Fleet diesel submarines are making for their assigned patrol areas.
NK-04.scene: Morning light comes into the room after the all-night session. You have said the result is half a success and half not. It is good that the whole world is now looking at Cuba, and in time, if need be, the weapons can be sent again. The problem is the sea. Once the quarantine line (the naval cordon that stops ships bound for Cuba) takes effect, the U.S. Navy will stop Soviet ships and board them. If the ships do not stop, vessels flying the Soviet flag may be fired on on the high seas; if they turn back, the world will write that the Soviet Union retreated. Malinovsky reads out the ships’ positions one by one: ships in the Mediterranean, ships in mid-Atlantic, and the Aleksandrovsk, a day out from Cuba. Whether to publish the treaty must also be raised again.

voices.who: Nikita Khrushchev (your words, as recorded in the Malin notes)
voices.text: Half a success, and half not. That the whole world has fixed its attention on Cuba is positive. In time, and if it is needed, it will be sent again.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: Turn the ships back and we show the world the blockade worked. The high seas are not America’s sea. Let the ships go on, and let the Americans know the submarines are behind them.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: If a ship carrying weapons is stopped on the high seas and its cargo photographed, we will have no choices left. Turn back the ships that are still far away, and let in only those that are close. What is already in Cuba is card enough to play.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: The Aleksandrovsk can make La Isabela or Mariel by tomorrow. The four submarines are still a day from their assigned areas, too far away to be given escort duty.

choices.text: Let the weapons ships sail on. Have the captains refuse any order to heave to, with the four submarines backing them up
choices.why: The belief that one retreat invites the next demand: a contest staked on the right of the high seas
choices.after: Orders went out to the captains to hold course. In the morning the U.S. Navy confirmed that the Soviet ships were not turning. At 10 a.m. (Washington) on 24 October the quarantine line took effect, and the first Soviet ship approached the interception line.

choices.text: Send the Mediterranean ships to the Black Sea and turn back the weapons ships still far off. Bring the Aleksandrovsk into the nearest port, and send the four submarines forward
choices.why: As long as the cargo is not photographed, the card stays in Cuba
choices.after: Everyone said it was right. Orders to turn back went to 16 ships, which swung their bows around at about 10 a.m. Moscow time; Washington would confirm it only the following morning. The Aleksandrovsk headed for the nearest port and the four submarines for their assigned areas. The decision not to publish the treaty was unanimous, and a cable was to go to Castro.

choices.text: Turn back every ship and recall the submarines too. Publish the treaty and show the world that the weapons in Cuba are there under it
choices.why: At sea we will lose, so fight with law and documents
choices.after: The order to turn back included the submarines, and the announcement of the treaty went out at noon. The Aleksandrovsk turned back into the Atlantic with her 24 warheads still aboard. In Havana Castro welcomed the publication of the treaty, but it was from Alekseev’s cable that he learned every ship had turned back.

note.text: The time of the order turning back the 16 ships is put at the morning of 23 October on the basis of the record kept by Captain Kidd of the U.S. Navy (“230800A,” that is, 3 a.m. in Washington and 10 a.m. in Moscow) and of Dobbs’s research. ExComm in Washington received the report that the ships had turned only during its meeting the next morning. No original text of Dobrynin’s cable has been published, so the content of the speech is given here in the form of a cable; the Aleksandrovsk’s port of arrival follows secondary sources.
