NK-05.time: 5 p.m. (10 a.m. in Washington, 9 a.m. in Havana)
NK-05.place: The Kremlin → the Bolshoi Theater, Moscow
NK-05.title: A Statement and an Opera

telegram.to: J. Kennedy, President of the United States of America
telegram.at: 23 October 1962, 5 p.m., for delivery to the US embassy in Moscow
telegram.subject: Reply to your letter of 22 October
telegram.text: I must say frankly that the measures indicated in your statement constitute a serious threat to the peace and security of peoples. / The United States arrogates to itself the right to decide what weapons the Republic of Cuba may consider necessary for its defense, and seeks to dictate to other states. / The Soviet Union confirms that the armaments now in Cuba, regardless of the classification to which they belong, are destined exclusively for defensive purposes.

NK-05.event: In the morning the Soviet government issued a statement accusing the United States of preparing a third world war. The Defense Ministry postponed the discharge of servicemen in the Strategic Rocket Forces, the Air Defense Forces and the submarine fleet, and canceled all leave. In New York the Security Council meets at 4 p.m. (Washington) today, where Ambassador Zorin will face the American resolution. In Washington, Kennedy signs the quarantine proclamation this evening.
NK-05.scene: Gromyko has brought the draft of the letter to Kennedy. It condemns the blockade and affirms that the weapons are for defense. You insisted on the words “regardless of the classification to which they belong,” which neither deny nor admit the missiles. Troyanovsky is holding tickets for “Boris Godunov” at the Bolshoi tonight. The American bass Jerome Hines is singing Tsar Boris, and foreign correspondents will be there. If you are seen in the theater, the world will write that all is normal in Moscow. Kozlov says this is a night for the command post, not the theater.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister)
voices.text: The letter should stop there. Condemning the blockade and affirming that the weapons are defensive is enough. Bring in Berlin or Turkey, and the Americans will read it as the Soviet Union raising the stakes.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: Kennedy spoke to his own people. The Soviet people must see where the First Secretary is, too. And it should not be at the opera.

voices.who: Oleg Troyanovsky (aide)
voices.text: Go to the theater. One photograph of you raising a glass with an American singer will travel further than ten statements. I will bring you the cables in the intervals.

choices.text: Send the letter but skip the theater. Hold an all-night Presidium session and see personally to the combat readiness of Pliyev’s forces and the ships
choices.why: Focus: let friend and foe alike see the leader at his post
choices.after: The meeting went on until dawn, with no fresh news. Foreign news agencies reported that the lights in the Kremlin had burned all night. Kennedy’s reply arrived the next morning; the quarantine line takes effect at 5 p.m. (Moscow) that day.

choices.text: Send the letter as it stands and condemn the blockade in a statement. In the evening watch “Boris Godunov” at the Bolshoi to show that all is normal
choices.why: A photograph shows you are not afraid better than words can
choices.after: The letter was delivered to the American embassy at 5 p.m. That night you sat in the Bolshoi’s state box and raised a glass of champagne with Hines. The next morning Kennedy’s reply was on your desk. The blockade takes effect at 5 p.m. (Moscow) that day.

choices.text: Raise the question of access to West Berlin in the letter as well, to let the Americans know that Cuba and Berlin are one game
choices.why: Press where America hurts, and the price of the blockade goes up
choices.after: Berlin went into the last paragraph of the letter. Washington read it as a threat, and the American garrison in West Berlin was put on alert. Two days later Western traffic began to slow at the East German checkpoints.

note.text: The letter of 23 October is in FRUS VI d61 (Moscow cable 1042), in the embassy’s translation. The 5 p.m. delivery follows the sending time of embassy cable 1042 (5 p.m., 23 October, Moscow); the letter reached the White House at 11:05 a.m. (Washington) on the 23rd. The visit to the Bolshoi and the toast with Hines come from a secondary source, the National Security Archive’s commentary (doc 29385). The postponed discharges and canceled leave are confirmed by the report of Malinovsky and Yepishev of 24 October (CWIHP Bulletin 5); the original of the combat readiness order of 23 October has not been published. The Berlin option does not appear in the Presidium notes; it is a hypothetical choice drawn only from the concerns voiced in Western documents.
note.src: FRUS VI d61; NSA doc 29385; Bulletin 5 p.74; Phase 1 ending logic H

NK-06.time: 3 p.m. (8 a.m. in Washington, 7 a.m. in Havana)
NK-06.place: First Secretary’s office, the Kremlin, Moscow
NK-06.title: Ultimatum
NK-06.clock: 2 hours until the quarantine line takes effect (10 a.m. in Washington, 5 p.m. in Moscow)

telegram.subject: Visit of Attorney General R. Kennedy to the embassy (night of 23 October)
telegram.text: The President felt he had been deceived, and deceived deliberately. R. Kennedy returned again and again to my assurance to him in September that there were no long-range missiles in Cuba. / R. Kennedy: “I don’t know how all this will end, for we intend to stop your ships.” / My comment: if necessary, the R. Kennedy channel could be used to convey Comrade N. S. Khrushchev’s thinking unofficially.

NK-06.event: Kennedy’s reply came in the morning. It reminded you that the Soviet Union had given assurances in September that there were no missiles, and it demanded that Soviet ships observe the quarantine. In New York the acting secretary-general, U Thant, is preparing to appeal to the two leaders this evening for a voluntary suspension of two to three weeks. William Knox, president of Westinghouse International, is in Moscow and wants to see you.
NK-06.scene: Kennedy’s letter and Dobrynin’s cable lie side by side on your desk. Kennedy wrote that you should have Soviet ships follow the U.S. Navy’s instructions. You say that this is not a quarantine but an ultimatum: the Soviet government cannot instruct Soviet captains to obey the orders of American warships. The ships turned back yesterday, so the problem now is words. Gromyko hands you a draft reply, and Mikoyan says to speak harshly and keep the ships back. Troyanovsky advises you to give Knox three hours. Tell an American businessman, not a diplomat, that the missiles are there, and within a day it will be in the White House.

voices.who: Anatoly Dobrynin (ambassador in Washington, cable)
voices.text: The President felt he had been deceived, and deceived deliberately. Robert Kennedy said: “I don’t know how all this will end, for we intend to stop your ships.”

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister)
voices.text: The reply should concentrate on the blockade being a violation of international law and an ultimatum. We write that we cannot order the captains to obey, but say nothing about what we will do with the ships. They have already turned back, after all.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: U Thant issues his appeal tonight. If we accept it, stopping the ships becomes not a Soviet decision but a response to a UN request. It is a way to buy a day without losing face.

voices.who: Oleg Troyanovsky (aide)
voices.text: Knox is no friend of Kennedy’s, but he will report straight to Rusk. Let him be the one to carry it: the missiles are there, but they will not be fired without the First Secretary’s personal order.

choices.text: Keep the reply short and wait for U Thant’s appeal. Publicly instruct the captains to stop outside the interception line, so that it looks like compliance with a UN request
choices.why: The same retreat saves face if it takes the form of answering a UN request
choices.after: U Thant’s first appeal came out that evening, and the next day you replied, “I agree with your proposal.” The order for Soviet captains to wait outside the interception area was made public. Kennedy answered that the work was still going on. You had bought a day, but the missiles in Cuba stayed where they were.

choices.text: Answer Kennedy that this is an “ultimatum,” and tell Knox that the missiles are there but will not be fired without the First Secretary’s order
choices.why: A move with two faces: no retreat in public, while the back door tells the Americans there is nothing to fear
choices.after: The reply went out that evening. It called the blockade “outright banditry” and said the Soviet Union would not simply stand by and watch acts of piracy by American ships on the high seas. You saw Knox for three hours. You told him the missiles would be used only to defend Cuba and only on your personal instruction, and that Guantánamo would disappear on the first day. Knox’s report reached Rusk on 26 October.

choices.text: Order the captains to refuse to heave to and to run the quarantine line, with the submarine brigade as escort, so that the U.S. Navy has to fire first
choices.why: A gamble that whoever fires first on the high seas loses in the eyes of the world
choices.after: Two of the ships that had turned back yesterday swung their bows toward Cuba again. At 5 p.m. (Moscow) the quarantine line took effect. A U.S. destroyer ordered the first ship to heave to, and the captain, as instructed, held his speed.

note.text: The letter of 24 October is in FRUS VI d63 (“outright banditry” and “piracy” are its words). Kennedy’s letter of 23 October was sent at 6:51 p.m. Washington time and reached Moscow before dawn on the 24th; the three-hour length of the Knox meeting comes from the National Security Archive’s commentary, based on Knox’s report. The content of the Knox meeting appears only in excerpt in that commentary (doc 29385, from Defense Department Cuba files), so the text gives only its gist. Dobrynin’s cable of 24 October is printed in CWIHP Bulletin 5, which gives no cable number.
note.src: FRUS VI d63; Dobrynin 10/24 (Bulletin 5); NSA doc 29385 (excerpt)

NK-H1.time: 11 p.m. (4 p.m. in Washington, 3 p.m. in Havana)
NK-H1.title: The Quarantine Line
NK-H1.event: The quarantine line took effect at 5 p.m. (Moscow). In the evening a U.S. destroyer ordered a Soviet freighter to heave to, and the captain, as instructed, held his speed. The destroyer fired a warning shot across her bow, and a second shot grazed the wheelhouse. When the captain stopped engines, an American boarding party came aboard and opened up the cargo. The photographs will be in Washington within hours.
NK-H1.scene: Malinovsky’s report reaches the night session. The boarded ship was carrying missile fuel and spare parts, and the ships behind her have slowed. The four submarines are still 300 miles short of their assigned areas north of the Bahamas, too far away to be given escort duty. In New York U Thant has appealed to both leaders for a voluntary suspension of two to three weeks. Gromyko proposes using the appeal as the form in which to stop the ships. Kozlov wants to pay back in Berlin what was suffered in Cuban waters. Mikoyan says a photograph of one ship must not become a reason for war.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: The submarines have not reached their assigned areas, and because of their batteries they have to surface every night. Give them escort duty and they will only be found and hunted. At sea we cannot help but lose.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister)
voices.text: If we answer U Thant’s appeal with “I agree,” stopping the ships becomes compliance with a UN request. The reply must go out tonight.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: America’s sore spot is not the Caribbean but Berlin. Close the access routes through East Germany, and the Americans will be worrying not about ships off Cuba but about their garrison in West Berlin.

choices.text: Rather than give ground in Cuban waters, order controls on the West Berlin access routes through East Germany and change what the Americans have to worry about
choices.why: When a game is going against you, a leader’s job is to open another
choices.after: Before midnight the order went to the Soviet forces in East Germany. On the morning of 25 October Western military traffic came to a stop at the Helmstedt checkpoint. Washington had to spread out two maps at once.

choices.text: Stop the ships and turn them back. Step back in the form of agreeing to U Thant’s appeal, and save face
choices.why: Caution: you cannot start a war over a photograph of one ship
choices.after: Before dawn the reply to U Thant went out. The ships withdrew beyond the interception area, and the boarded ship turned for home once the Americans had left her. American newspapers wrote that a Soviet ship had submitted to search on the high seas. At the next day’s Presidium session you had to decide your next move.

choices.text: Authorize the submarine brigade to engage as escorts. If a ship flying the Soviet flag is attacked again on the high seas, they are to return fire
choices.why: If a Soviet ship is hit and no one fires back, the next ship will be hit too
choices.after: The Main Naval Staff sent the brigade its authorization to engage, but amid the jamming it was a day before anyone could confirm which submarines had received the order intact. Meanwhile the U.S. Navy found B-130, which had surfaced with diesel trouble, and began hunting the other submarines.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact 16 ships turned back on the morning of 23 October, and no Soviet ship was fired on or boarded at the quarantine line. Running the blockade was an option raised at the Presidium on 23 October. The positions of the four submarines and the delays in communication follow the Northern Fleet report and Arkhipov’s 1997 presentation.
note.src: Malin 10/23; Arkhipov 1997; Northern Fleet report 1962-12

NK-H10.title: Torpedo in the Sargasso
NK-H10.event: During the night, in the Sargasso Sea, a Soviet submarine took an American destroyer’s depth charges for an attack and fired a conventional torpedo. The destroyer was holed and lost a number of her crew, and a carrier group sank the submarine a few hours later. Washington has demanded that Soviet ships and submarines pull back from the interception line within 24 hours, and the U.S. Air Force has doubled its low-level reconnaissance over Cuba.
NK-H10.scene: The chief of the Main Naval Staff comes in with a brief report. It is not yet known which submarine it was, or whether any of the 78 men aboard have been rescued. American radio is talking of a Soviet attack on the high seas, and the Security Council meets again tonight. Malinovsky reports that two of the three R-12 regiments in Cuba have completed launch preparations. Mikoyan says that unless the clash is declared an accident and a withdrawal proposal put forward today, there will be nothing left to offer tomorrow. Kozlov says that with Soviet sailors dead there can be no retreat. Gromyko suggests cautiously that raising Berlin could draw American eyes away from the sea.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: Nikita Sergeyevich, if the letter goes today, the accident stays an accident. Wait another day, and the Americans will have their pretext for bombing Cuba and will not even read the letter.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: The two R-12 regiments can fire within hours of an order. But the moment they fire, the Soviet homeland takes the reply. Firing from Cuba and being hit in the Soviet Union are one and the same decision.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: There are 78 sailors in the sea. We have to explain to the Soviet people why they died. A letter offering withdrawal explains nothing.

choices.text: Retaliate. Order the R-12 regiments in Cuba to prepare to launch, and raise the alert of the Strategic Rocket Forces so that the Americans stop
choices.why: Anger: leave the sailors’ deaths unanswered, and the next demand will come
choices.after: Half a day after the order went out, a U.S. Air Force reconnaissance plane photographed missiles on their launchers. Washington read it as preparation to launch. What happened in the 48 hours after that is told in the Ending.

choices.text: Declare the clash an accident and send a letter proposing immediate withdrawal in exchange for a pledge of no invasion
choices.why: There is only one day in which an accident can be ended as an accident
choices.after: The letter was delivered to the American embassy that night. The Soviet government regretted that the submarine commander, judging himself under attack, had fired back; it would send no more weapons to Cuba, and given an American pledge of no invasion, the reason for its military specialists to remain would also disappear. Kennedy held back his answer, and the next day you had to rewrite the letter.

choices.text: Win back in Berlin what was lost at sea. Close the access routes through East Germany and make the Americans watch two places at once
choices.why: What is lost in one place can be won back in another
choices.after: In the evening the order went to the Soviet forces in East Germany. The next morning Western military vehicles came to a halt between Helmstedt and Marienborn. Washington had to spread out two maps at once.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact, on the night of 25 October B-130 merely surfaced with diesel trouble and was detected; no Soviet submarine fired a torpedo. The crew of 78 is the figure for B-59, and each Foxtrot-class submarine carried 21 conventional torpedoes and one nuclear torpedo.
note.src: Northern Fleet report 1962-12; Arkhipov 1997; Phase 1 issue 3

map.caption: The four Foxtrot-class submarines were deployed to assigned patrol areas in the Sargasso Sea, outside the quarantine line.

NK-H2.time: Morning (night of the 25th in Washington and Havana)
NK-H2.title: Berlin
NK-H2.event: A day has passed since Western military traffic was blocked at the Helmstedt checkpoint. The United States, Britain and France have sent notes of protest, and the American garrison in West Berlin is on alert. The NATO Council sat through the night in Paris. Kennedy had warned in advance that whatever happened over Cuba could have repercussions in Berlin.
NK-H2.scene: Two maps are spread on the table: the Caribbean and Berlin. Gromyko recalls the blockade of 1948. Then the West held out for 11 months by airlift, and the Soviet Union lifted the blockade with nothing gained. Malinovsky says that if Western forces push their way down the access routes, fighting will begin on East German soil and spread across Europe faster than anything at sea off Cuba. Kozlov says that if America can be made to fire first in both places, the world will see America as the aggressor. Mikoyan wants to fold the two games into one and bargain: decide what to get in Berlin as the price of taking the missiles out of Cuba.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister)
voices.text: In 1948 Stalin blocked Berlin and got nothing. This time is different, because we hold the missiles in Cuba. We can put both questions into one letter and make the Americans negotiate on both.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: If the West pushes down the access routes with armored cars, our forces in East Germany will have to fire. In Cuba there is an ocean in between; in Berlin it is 100 meters. A war that starts in Europe has nowhere to stop.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: Does America have the right to blockade Cuba while the Soviet Union has no right to blockade Berlin? Keep both. Whoever fires first is the loser in the eyes of the world.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: Drag both crises along together and we lose both. Lift the controls on the access routes and, in return, put withdrawal from Cuba and a pledge of no invasion into one letter. Then it is not a retreat but a deal.

choices.text: Keep the controls and leave the missiles in Cuba. Make America fire first in both places and cast it as the aggressor
choices.why: A gamble that if you hold firm in both places, America cannot strike in either
choices.after: The access routes were still closed when November came. The airlift to West Berlin began again, and the blockade in the Caribbean went on. No first shot was fired in either place, but the two crises went into the winter together.

choices.text: Lift the access controls and offer withdrawal from Cuba as part of the exchange. Put both crises in one letter and make America negotiate on both
choices.why: Fold two games into one, and even a retreat becomes a deal
choices.after: In the morning the barrier at Helmstedt went up. You sat in your office and dictated a long letter to Kennedy. Berlin survived only in the last paragraph; the body of the letter was Cuba.

choices.text: Keep the controls, revive the 1958 demand for a free city of Berlin, and propose a summit to deal with Cuba and Berlin
choices.why: Keep the crisis open while drawing the other side to the table
choices.after: Washington rejected the summit proposal: there could be no meeting while the missiles were in Cuba. Another day passed with the access routes half open and the missiles in Cuba where they were.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. The Presidium notes contain no option of blockading Berlin; a countermove in Berlin appears only among the concerns voiced in Western documents, such as those of McNamara and Macmillan. The Berlin blockade of 1948–49 and the free-city demand of 1958 are historical facts, and the figures are those commonly cited.
note.src: Phase 1 ending logic H; Malin 10/22~28

map.caption: West Berlin was an island inside East Germany, linked to West Germany by three land routes and three air corridors.

NK-07.time: Morning (before dawn on the 25th in Washington and Havana)
NK-07.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, Presidium meeting room
NK-07.title: The Wooden Knife

telegram.from: Zorin (New York, Soviet mission to the UN)
telegram.subject: Security Council session and U Thant’s appeal
telegram.text: Stevenson displayed aerial photographs in the chamber, alleged launch sites in Cuba. I replied they were fabrications of American intelligence. / Stevenson demanded a “yes or no”. I answered that this is not an American courtroom. / U Thant has appealed to both governments to suspend arms shipments and the quarantine voluntarily for two to three weeks. American side wants a second appeal (Soviet ships to hold outside the interception area, US to avoid confrontation).

NK-07.event: Kennedy answered U Thant’s first appeal by saying the problem was the missiles. At the quarantine line the Soviet tanker Bucharest was let through without inspection. From Havana, Alekseev reported that Castro fully approves Soviet tactics and judges that the United States does not now have enough strength for a surprise attack. The Aleksandrovsk, which was close to Cuba, has entered port carrying 24 warheads for the R-14.
NK-07.scene: You speak first, before dictating a letter to the Presidium. Do not get drawn into petty squabbling, trading insult for insult. Get a pledge from Kennedy not to touch Cuba; in return, dismantle the missile sites and allow UN inspection. This is not capitulation. If we fire, they fire back. The Americans are plainly frightened. Kennedy has been sleeping with a wooden knife under his pillow. Mikoyan asks why a wooden knife, and you tell the story of the man going bear hunting for the first time. The joke is later struck through in Serov’s notes. You also raise the possibility of pulling out only the R-12s and leaving the other missiles: the United States can be hit from Soviet territory as well, so there is no need to hurry. On the table lies a query from the Defense Ministry asking whether to turn back the ships carrying the special cargo.

voices.who: Nikita Khrushchev (your words as recorded in Malin’s notes)
voices.text: Do not get drawn into petty squabbling, repaying insult with the same arguments. Write a letter to Kennedy as I dictate it. We will dismantle the missile sites. We have made Cuba a country on which the attention of the world is fixed. If you give a pledge not to touch Cuba, we will agree to dismantle and will allow UN inspectors to verify it.

voices.who: Nikita Khrushchev (your words as recorded in Serov’s notes)
voices.text: Perhaps this is what we must do. This is not capitulation, because if we fire, they will fire too. There is no doubt the Americans are frightened, that much is clear. Kennedy has been sleeping with a wooden knife.

voices.who: Nikita Khrushchev (your words as recorded in Serov’s notes)
voices.text: We must play the game, but without losing our heads. The initiative is in our hands and there is nothing to fear. We started this and then got frightened. Fighting is not in our interest. The future depends not on Cuba but on the Soviet Union.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: If Kennedy is frightened, let him be the one to back down first. The blockade only stops ships, and the missiles are already in Cuba. A few more days and they will be ready to fire.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister)
voices.text: For the reply to U Thant, I suggest we set aside the ministry’s draft and simply say “I agree with your proposal.” And we should have Zorin vote for the resolution from Ghana and the United Arab Republic.

choices.text: Leave the missiles in place and stand firm. Kennedy is plainly frightened, so ride out the blockade and let the regiments in Cuba finish their launch preparations
choices.why: A gambler’s calculation: it is foolish to back down when the other side has blinked first
choices.after: No letter was written. The Aleksandrovsk’s warheads stayed in port. That evening Kennedy said the blockade was working and that work on the sites was continuing. The next day the US Air Force stepped up low-level reconnaissance to twice a day.

choices.text: Bargain for a deal that withdraws only the R-12s and keeps the R-14s. The United States can be hit from Soviet territory anyway, so play for time with the R-14s as the condition
choices.why: The calculation that giving up half and keeping half is the basis of any trade
choices.after: Gromyko drafted a two-stage withdrawal. But Malinovsky pointed out that not a single R-14 was yet in Cuba, only the warheads aboard ship, and the meeting dragged on. No letter went out that day, and the Americans announced that work on the sites was continuing.

choices.text: Dictate the letter. If Kennedy pledges not to touch Cuba, dismantle the missile sites and allow UN inspection. Turn the Aleksandrovsk around
choices.why: The calculation that admits you will be hit if you fire, but seeks a price for it: no invasion of Cuba
choices.after: Every member and secretary of the Presidium backed you. The ships carrying the special cargo were to be turned back. Malinovsky instructed Pliyev that the 665th and 668th regiments would not be sent, that the Aleksandrovsk’s R-14 warheads were not to be unloaded, and that if they had been, they were to be reloaded in secret. U Thant was told “I agree with your proposal.” The letter to Kennedy would be polished again the next day.

choices.text: Build on U Thant’s proposal for a two- to three-week freeze. Instead of the ministry’s draft, reply “I agree with your proposal” and leave the negotiation to the UN
choices.why: The calculation that with the UN in between you gain time and save face
choices.after: The reply to U Thant went out in the afternoon, and Zorin made public the order for ships to hold outside the interception area. The letter to Kennedy was put off. In New York, Stevenson began to speak of negotiations conditional on a 24- to 48-hour halt to work on the sites.

note.text: Two records of the 25 October meeting survive: Malin’s notes (Protocol No. 61) and Serov’s notes. The bear-hunting joke is a passage struck through and deleted in Serov’s notes. The remarks “let us leave the other missiles and take out only the R-12s” and “we can strike the United States from Soviet territory” also follow in Serov’s notes as your words. The Bucharest’s passage is in the ExComm record for the morning of 25 October (Washington). The Trostnik-to-Pavlov cable of 25 October (665th and 668th regiments not to be sent, warheads to be reloaded) is Wilson Center 117324. The first sentence of Zorin’s cable (the claim that the photographs were faked) is in Bulletin 5; the rest renders the Security Council record (S/PV.1025) in cable form.
note.src: Malin 10/25; Serov 10/25; WC/UMD 117324; Zorin 10/25 (Bulletin 5); Alekseev 10/23; FRUS XI d63

pressure.title: Not Capitulation
pressure.text: On the morning of 25 October your mind was made up before you sat down with the Presidium. Kennedy had chosen a blockade, not a landing or an air strike, and to you that was proof the Americans were frightened. You began by saying this was not capitulation: if we fire, they fire back; and Kennedy had been sleeping with a wooden knife, the kind a man takes on his first bear hunt, for when he soils his trousers. Serov’s notes also preserve your remarks that we started this and then got frightened, that fighting is not in our interest, and that the future depends on the Soviet Union, not Cuba. Since you defeated the anti-party group in 1957 no one in the Presidium had stood against you, and the notes record that on this day too every member and secretary supported you. But you still had no words with which to present the removal of the missiles to the Presidium and the socialist camp as a victory.

NK-H6.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, Presidium meeting room
NK-H6.title: The Freeze
NK-H6.event: To U Thant’s second appeal you replied that you would hold your ships outside the interception area, and Kennedy replied that in that case US warships would avoid a confrontation. In New York, Stevenson is talking of negotiations conditional on a 24- to 48-hour halt to work on the sites, and U Thant is drawing up a plan to send UN observers to Cuba during a two- to three-week freeze. The hawks in Washington say a freeze favors only the Soviet Union so long as construction in Cuba goes on.
NK-H6.scene: Reports from the UN pile up in the meeting room. Zorin expects that once freeze negotiations begin, the Americans will spend weeks maintaining the blockade while world opinion tilts toward the Soviet Union. Malinovsky says that if construction at the launch sites continues at night, the longer the talks run the more launchers will be ready. Mikoyan warns that if that is discovered, U Thant too will turn away and Kennedy will have his pretext for bombing. Gromyko says a letter straight to Kennedy is faster than the UN’s long table. You must decide between the UN’s time and Cuba’s launchers.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister)
voices.text: The UN is slow. During two weeks of freeze the Americans will photograph Cuba every day, and one photograph will end the freeze. A letter written directly to Kennedy is faster and surer.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: A freeze stops the American blockade too. Meanwhile Pliyev can carry on construction at night. In two weeks all 24 R-12s will be standing on their launchers.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: If we accept a freeze, we must keep it. If we are photographed carrying on construction at night, we lose U Thant as well. Accept the observers and leave the missiles where they are until the talks are over.

choices.text: Accept the freeze but continue construction in Cuba at night. The longer the talks run, the more launchers will be ready
choices.why: The calculation that the negotiating table exists to buy time
choices.after: The order for night work went to Pliyev. Two days later a US Air Force low-level reconnaissance aircraft photographed a newly erected launcher, and Stevenson displayed the picture in the Security Council. U Thant’s freeze collapsed on the spot.

choices.text: Set the freeze aside and write directly to Kennedy. Propose trading a pledge not to invade Cuba for withdrawal of the missiles
choices.why: The judgment that two men speaking directly is faster than the UN’s long table
choices.after: You replied to U Thant that you continued to support the UN’s efforts, and in your office you dictated a letter to Kennedy. It was delivered to the US embassy that afternoon.

choices.text: Halt construction and accept UN observers. Leave the missiles where they are until the talks end and seek a settlement within the UN framework
choices.why: The belief that with the UN standing between them, neither the Americans nor the Soviets can easily fire first
choices.after: Pliyev was ordered to stop all construction and keep the camouflage in place. U Thant left for Havana with military technicians from neutral countries. Castro took three days to accept the observers, and the negotiations ran on into November.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact you answered U Thant on 25 October with “I agree with your proposal” (SG/1357), and on 26 October replied that you would hold your ships outside the interception area, but that same day you wrote directly to Kennedy and moved the center of the negotiation to the two of you. Stevenson’s proposal of a 24- to 48-hour halt to work was in fact discussed in ExComm on 26 October.
note.src: Malin 10/25; Phase 1 crossing point ⑥; Phase 1 ending logic E

NK-H3.time: Morning (before dawn on the 27th in Washington and Havana)
NK-H3.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, Presidium meeting room
NK-H3.title: Staying On
NK-H3.clock: About five hours until the American low-level reconnaissance flights (morning in Havana)

telegram.at: Received before dawn, 27 October 1962 (morning in Moscow)
telegram.subject: Night meeting with F. Castro
telegram.text: Castro considers intervention almost inevitable, within roughly 24 to 72 hours. Either an air strike or a full invasion, one or the other. / Castro spent the night at the embassy drafting a letter to Comrade N. S. Khrushchev. Transmitting by cable. / Cuban forces on full alert. 50 anti-aircraft batteries reassigned to protect Soviet positions.

NK-H3.event: Kennedy has gone two days without a letter from the Soviet Union. In Washington a plan to extend the blockade to oil and a plan for an air strike are both on the table, and US Air Force low-level reconnaissance has gone up to twice a day. A landing force is massing in Florida. In Havana, Castro is certain of an attack within 24 to 72 hours and has spent the night writing to you.
NK-H3.scene: Alekseev’s cable and Malinovsky’s intelligence report lie on the table. The US Navy maintains the blockade and the US Air Force photographs Cuba daily. Today all 24 of the R-12 regiment’s missiles in Cuba became ready to fire. Malinovsky says they are ready, but if an American air strike comes, the launchers will be gone within hours. Mikoyan says that if you hold out longer, the Americans will move from blockade to bombing, and then an offer to withdraw becomes a letter of surrender. Kozlov says the Americans have failed to shoot for three days and will fail in future too. Gromyko says cautiously that now is the time to send the letter put off on 25 October.

voices.who: Aleksandr Alekseev (ambassador to Cuba, by cable)
voices.text: Castro considers intervention almost inevitable and expects it within roughly 24 to 72 hours.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: From today all 24 R-12s can fire on order. But missiles we will not fire will vanish from their launchers on the first day of an air strike. If we hold out, we must decide what we are holding out for.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: Kennedy has waited three days because he was waiting for a letter. If we do not send it today, what comes next will not be a letter but bombs.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: In three days the Americans have not stopped a single ship or dropped a single bomb. The blockade can last until winter, and so can the missiles in Cuba.

choices.text: Ride out the blockade. If the Americans only blockade and cannot bring themselves to shoot, the missiles stay in Cuba through the winter and become a card to play over Berlin
choices.why: The judgment that an adversary who failed to shoot for three days will not shoot later either
choices.after: Again no letter went out. That afternoon a U-2 fell to a Soviet anti-aircraft missile over Cuba, and Washington met through the night. Kennedy chose to keep the blockade rather than strike back. The missiles stayed in Cuba.

choices.text: Offer withdrawal now. Send the proposal put off on 25 October as a letter and trade it for a pledge not to invade
choices.why: The calculation that missiles you will not fire should fetch a price before they are lost to bombing
choices.after: The letter was delivered to the US embassy that evening. It was two days late, and in the meantime an air-strike timetable had been laid on the table in Washington. The next morning you had to decide whether to add Turkey.

choices.text: Give Pliyev discretion to use tactical nuclear weapons in the event of a landing and keep the R-12s ready to fire. If an invasion comes, finish it on the beaches
choices.why: The judgment that the one weapon able to stop an invasion should be in the hands of the man on the spot
choices.after: The directive left unsigned in September went to Havana by cipher cable. Pliyev confirmed receipt, and the Luna battalion’s special warheads were moved up close to the launchers. That afternoon the U-2 fell, and Washington waited no longer.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact you sent the “knot” letter on 26 October. Alekseev’s cable of 27 October (Castro’s 24- to 72-hour forecast, the drafting of his letter) is printed in full in CWIHP Bulletin 17/18; the figure of 50 Cuban anti-aircraft batteries comes from Castro’s letter of 28 October. The date on which all 24 R-12s became ready to fire follows the Statsenko division report. Leaving the missiles in place was in fact raised at the Presidium on 25 October.
note.src: Alekseev 10/27 (Bulletin 17/18); WC/UMD 300465; Serov 10/25; Phase 1 ending logic F

NK-H7.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, Presidium meeting room
NK-H7.title: Missiles in Winter
NK-H7.event: The blockade is in its fourth week. The Americans did not bomb Cuba even after the U-2 was shot down; they keep up low-level reconnaissance and nothing more. Every Soviet ship bound for Cuba is holding outside the interception area. The talks in New York are stuck on inspection, and Castro refuses any inspection at all. In Washington the demands to extend the blockade to oil and to launch an air strike grow louder each week. In West Berlin, checks on the access routes have begun to slow.
NK-H7.scene: Snow falls on the Kremlin, and the same men as a month ago sit in the meeting room. The missiles are in Cuba, the blockade is at sea, and no one has fired. Malinovsky says the 24 R-12s are ready to fire, but not one R-14 has got through, and he worries about the Group of Forces facing winter with its supplies cut off. Gromyko believes the Americans are drifting toward tacit acceptance of the missiles while keeping the blockade, and that the price can be collected over Berlin in the spring of 1963. Mikoyan warns that the Americans will never permanently tolerate missiles without inspection, and that come spring the decision will be made not by Kennedy but by Congress.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister)
voices.text: The Americans are in a position where they can neither lift the blockade nor shoot. If we open Berlin talks in the spring, the missiles in Cuba will be the biggest card on the table.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: Tacit acceptance is not a decision; it is a postponement. When Congress convenes in January, Kennedy can postpone no longer. Leave the missiles there all winter and in spring we get bombs, not a price.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: Forty thousand men of the Group of Forces will go through the winter without resupply. We keep them ready to fire, but the army is freezing to guard missiles we will not fire.

choices.text: Within November, offer to withdraw the R-12s but leave the Il-28s and the tactical weapons in Cuba. Get the blockade lifted and a pledge not to invade
choices.why: The calculation that giving up the biggest card and keeping the rest is the way to reach a deal, even late
choices.after: The offer was negotiated in New York for several more weeks, and the Americans would not accept a withdrawal without inspection. The blockade ran into the new year, and the checks around Berlin grew slower still.

choices.text: Leave the missiles in place under the blockade and link them to Berlin talks in the spring of 1963. Do not play the card while the Americans tolerate it
choices.why: The calculation that the missile you do not fire is the most valuable missile of all
choices.after: Through the winter the missiles stayed in Cuba and the blockade stayed at sea. In the spring of 1963 the next crisis began on the access routes to Berlin.

choices.text: Authorize Pliyev to shoot down the low-level reconnaissance aircraft, to force the lifting of the blockade. The daily photographs are the Americans’ card
choices.why: The gamble that if you blind the other side, it will come to the table first
choices.after: Three days later two American reconnaissance aircraft fell over Cuba. Kennedy waited no longer. The air strikes began, and what followed is told in the Ending.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact Kennedy announced the lifting of the blockade on 20 November, and the same day Malinovsky ordered Pliyev to return 6 nuclear bombs, 12 Luna warheads and 80 FKR warheads aboard the Atkarsk. The link to a Berlin crisis in 1963 is a hypothesis following the planning document’s Ending F.
note.src: WC/UMD 117337; FRUS XI d196; Phase 1 ending logic F

NK-08.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, the First Secretary’s office
NK-08.title: The Knot

telegram.to: J. Kennedy, President of the United States of America
telegram.at: 26 October 1962, 4:43 p.m., for delivery to the US embassy in Moscow
telegram.subject: (no subject)
telegram.text: You and we ought not now to pull on the ends of the rope in which you have tied the knot of war, because the more the two of us pull, the tighter that knot will be tied. And a moment may come when that knot will be tied so tight that even he who tied it will not have the strength to untie it, and then it will be necessary to cut that knot. / The Soviet Union proposes. We declare that Soviet ships bound for Cuba will carry no armaments of any kind. You declare that the United States will not invade Cuba with its forces and will not support any sort of forces which might intend to carry out an invasion of Cuba. Then the necessity for the presence of our military specialists in Cuba would disappear.

NK-08.event: At the quarantine line, American sailors boarded and inspected the Lebanese-flag freighter Marucla. From Washington came a report that the KGB’s Fomin had met the ABC correspondent Scali and spoken of dismantling under UN supervision in exchange for a guarantee against invasion. From Havana, Alekseev reported that Castro fully approves Soviet tactics and judges that the United States does not have the strength for an immediate surprise attack.
NK-08.scene: You have not called the Presidium. In your office, before Troyanovsky and a stenographer, you dictate the letter. The substance is what the Presidium decided yesterday: trade a pledge not to invade Cuba for withdrawal of the missiles. But you do not say so directly; you take the long way around. Let us not pull together on the knot of war. Soviet ships will carry no more weapons, and if the United States undertakes not to invade, there will be no reason for Soviet military specialists to remain in Cuba. You avoid the word missile. Gromyko asks whether to include the American missiles in Turkey, and you say not yet. The letter is long, and it will take hours to translate, encode and get into Washington.

voices.who: Oleg Troyanovsky (aide)
voices.text: Nikita Sergeyevich, if we go this way, Washington will receive it in several sections, from 6 in the evening until 9 at night. If the heart of it is in the last section, they will have to wait three hours for it.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister)
voices.text: Better to leave Turkey out. Today we should speak only of Cuba, so that Kennedy can take this letter to his advisers. Turkey will not be too late in the next letter.

voices.who: Aleksandr Alekseev (ambassador to Cuba, cable of 23 October)
voices.text: Castro considers that the United States does not at present have sufficient forces for a surprise attack.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: If what Fomin told Scali and this letter arrive on the same day, the Americans will read it as the Soviet Union meaning it. The letter must go today.

choices.text: Add the withdrawal of the American missiles in Turkey to the letter as a condition. Put Cuba and Turkey in one sentence so the shape of the exchange is clear from the start
choices.why: The calculation that the Presidium will accept only a deal that looks like trading like for like
choices.after: The letter was delivered that evening with Turkey in it. Washington stopped at that sentence: the missiles of a NATO ally could not be bargained away to the Soviet Union. The next morning you had to decide again whether to leave the condition in.

choices.text: Hold the letter and wait a day to see whether an American answer comes first through the unofficial Fomin–Scali channel
choices.why: The calculation that face is saved if the answer comes through the back door before the official letter
choices.after: That evening Scali passed Fomin Rusk’s message that time was very urgent. But the unofficial channel was not an answer, and the letter went out a day late. The next morning Washington would receive two letters at once.

choices.text: Send the letter as it stands. Trade for a pledge not to invade Cuba, but do not mention Turkey or use the word missile
choices.why: The calculation that a deal begins only when it is written in words the other side can accept
choices.after: The letter was delivered to the US embassy at 4:43 p.m.; the first section reached Washington at 6 in the evening and the last at 9 at night. In a telephone call with Macmillan that night, Kennedy spoke of 48 hours. The next morning you would decide whether to raise Turkey.

note.text: The letter of 26 October is FRUS VI d65 (Moscow cable 1101), and the State Department footnote (FRUS XI d84) records delivery at 4:43 p.m. Moscow time and receipt at the department (first section 6 p.m., last section 9 p.m.). Kennedy’s mention of 48 hours in his call with Macmillan that night is in FRUS XI d87. Because the letter was written without convening the Presidium, there are no Malin notes. The Fomin–Scali contact is in the American record (FRUS XI d80, d85).
note.src: FRUS VI d65; Alekseev 10/23 (Bulletin 17/18); Phase 1 crossing point ⑦; FRUS XI d84; FRUS XI d87

pressure.title: A Letter Written Alone
pressure.text: On 26 October you dictated the letter without calling the Presidium. It set down the deal agreed the day before, but avoiding the word missile and taking the long way around through the image of the knot was both your habit of speech and a way of saving face. In your earlier letters to Kennedy you had called the blockade an ultimatum and said you could not order your captains to obey American warships, so you had to avoid the appearance of backing down within a day. The letter also recalled the Bay of Pigs; you knew Kennedy had admitted that episode was a mistake. It would take hours to translate and encode the letter and get it into Washington, and in the meantime you became the one waiting for an answer.
pressure.src: FRUS VI d65; FRUS VI d63; FRUS XI d29; FRUS XI d84

NK-09.time: Morning (before dawn on the 27th in Washington and Havana)
NK-09.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, Presidium meeting room
NK-09.title: Turkey
NK-09.clock: Seven hours until the scheduled radio broadcast (5 p.m.)

telegram.subject: F. Castro’s proposal
telegram.text: Castro proposes that the Soviet government state publicly that the Soviet weapons in Cuba are under Soviet control. Cuban leadership considers it necessary to refute the American claim that the weapons will pass into Cuban hands. / Cuban forces on full alert. Repeated low-level overflights during the night.

NK-09.event: Overnight, cables came in from the KGB’s Fomin in Washington and from Rio de Janeiro, and Alekseev reported Castro’s proposal. Malinovsky’s intelligence report says American landing forces are gathering in Florida but there is no sign that an invasion is imminent. There is still no reply from Kennedy to yesterday’s letter.
NK-09.scene: Overnight you have changed your mind. The Americans have not attacked Cuba, and that fact must go into the calculation. An invasion seems unlikely, but it cannot be guaranteed. Yet to take only a pledge not to invade Cuba in return for removing the missiles is too little. If you can also get the American bases in Turkey and Pakistan removed, you can end this as the victor. You put before the Presidium a second letter supplementing yesterday’s. The Americans worry about Cuba at 90 miles from their shores, yet Turkey sits right against the Soviet Union, with the sentries of the two sides looking at one another; if the Soviet Union removes its offensive means from Cuba, the United States should remove the same means from Turkey. Gromyko wants Pakistan left out. Mikoyan worries that broadcasting it on the radio will corner Kennedy in front of his allies. Kozlov says that is exactly why it should be made public.

voices.who: Nikita Khrushchev (your words as recorded in Malin’s notes)
voices.text: They will not go in for an invasion. But it cannot be guaranteed. We must take into account that the Americans have not attacked Cuba. And if in return we get the removal of the bases in Turkey and Pakistan, we will come out as the victors. We agree to verification when the missiles are taken out.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister)
voices.text: Pakistan must come out. The Jupiters in Turkey are American nuclear missiles on Turkish soil, so they pair with Cuba. If we put Pakistan in as well, the Americans will read it as the Soviet Union raising its price.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: If we put it out on the radio, Kennedy cannot sell Turkey in front of NATO. If we send it only through the embassy, he still has a way to accept it quietly.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: It must be public. When the world sees Cuba and Turkey side by side, what the Soviet Union removes becomes an exchange, not a retreat. The Presidium will accept it only on those terms.

choices.text: Leave yesterday’s letter as it is. Piling Turkey on top would unsettle yesterday’s offer and make it impossible for Kennedy to accept
choices.why: A merchant’s calculation: raise a price once named and the deal falls through
choices.after: No second letter was written. Washington drafted its reply to yesterday’s letter alone, and the American side never raised Turkey first. In the afternoon you had to decide on the cable to Pliyev.

choices.text: Demand the withdrawal of the bases in both Turkey and Pakistan, but do not broadcast it; send it only through the embassy, leaving Kennedy a way to accept quietly
choices.why: The calculation that you name your full price but leave the other side its face, or he will not accept
choices.after: The letter went only through the embassy. Washington read the word Pakistan as the Soviet Union raising its price, and wrote its reply to yesterday’s letter alone. In the afternoon Pliyev’s cable came up.

choices.text: Write a letter adding the withdrawal of the American missiles in Turkey and broadcast it on the radio at 5 p.m. Leave Pakistan out
choices.why: The calculation that the world must see like weapons being traded for like
choices.after: The Presidium settled the text of the letter and decided on a radio broadcast at 5 p.m. and release to the press. It also approved Alekseev’s proposal. The letter reached Washington first over Radio Moscow at 10 a.m. Washington time, and the White House spent the day deciding which to answer, yesterday’s letter or today’s.

note.text: Malin’s notes on the 27 October meeting (Protocol No. 62) are brief. They record the settling of the letter’s text, the 5 p.m. radio broadcast and “approval of Comrade Pavlov’s proposal,” and Kramer’s editorial note identifies the Pavlov here as Alekseev, not Pliyev. The National Security Archive holds a five-page scan from the same day titled “Instructions of the CC Presidium regarding Pliyev’s cable,” but the Phase 1 research could not decipher it, so the content of that instruction is left blank in this scene. The text of the letter is FRUS VI d66.
note.src: Malin 10/27; FRUS VI d66; Phase 1 issue 7

pressure.title: The Morning You Raised the Price
pressure.text: Overnight you reconsidered the fact that the Americans had not attacked Cuba. An invasion seemed unlikely but could not be guaranteed, and even so, if the price of removing the missiles was a single pledge not to invade, it was too little to lay before the Presidium and the socialist camp. If you could get the American bases in Turkey and Pakistan, you said, you could end this as a victory. The Turkish missiles you had thought of in Bulgaria became, five months on, a sentence in a letter, and you had that letter read to the world on the radio at 5 p.m. A public broadcast cornered Kennedy in front of his allies, but your own circumstance was that yesterday’s letter still sat in Washington without an answer. At 4:30 that afternoon Malinovsky sent Pliyev No. 76639, reconfirming the ban on any use of nuclear weapons without orders from Moscow, and that evening in Cuba a U-2 would fall without orders.
pressure.src: Malin 10/27; FRUS VI d66; WC/UMD 117326; Phase 1 issue 7

map.caption: The Jupiter missiles in Turkey, near Izmir, held the cities of the southern Soviet Union within range.

NK-10.time: 4:30 p.m. (9:30 a.m. in Washington, 8:30 a.m. in Havana)
NK-10.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, Defense Ministry liaison office
NK-10.title: No. 76639
NK-10.clock: Thirty minutes until the radio broadcast (5 p.m.)

telegram.subject: Reply to your No. 8/154
telegram.text: We categorically confirm that use of nuclear weapons from the missiles, the FKRs, the “Lunas” and the aircraft without orders from Moscow is forbidden. / Confirm receipt.

NK-10.event: Pliyev’s cable No. 8/154 has come up. Reports from Havana say the Cubans expect an air strike tonight or tomorrow, that Castro has decided to open anti-aircraft fire if attacked, and that Pliyev too has resolved to use every means of air defense if an attack comes. In Havana the air-defense radars have been switched on since yesterday, and the warheads of Sidorov’s regiment have been moved up close to the launch sites.
NK-10.scene: Malinovsky has come in with three draft replies. One is No. 76639, categorically confirming the ban on nuclear use; one orders all work on the R-12 and R-14 sites halted, with camouflage work at night only; one orders the Aleksandrovsk home together with the Bratsk. In thirty minutes you put out over the radio a letter proposing the Turkey exchange. If a nuclear weapon is used in Cuba while that letter is going out, everything is finished. Kozlov argues the opposite: if an air strike is coming, Pliyev’s hands cannot be left empty; revive the September draft. Mikoyan says that if construction continues, the Soviet word at the UN becomes a lie.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: Pliyev says he will use every means of air defense. Conventional air defense is his discretion, but nuclear is not. If an air strike comes, everything on the ground will look like an airborne assault, so the ban has to be written out again and sent today.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: If the Americans bomb tonight, the R-12s vanish from their launchers and the Lunas vanish from their stores. If a landing comes, it stops only if Pliyev can fire. The September draft is in the safe.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: In thirty minutes the Soviet Union tells the world it will remove the missiles. If construction is still going on in Cuba at that hour, neither U Thant nor Kennedy will believe a Soviet word. The work must stop today.

choices.text: Forbid nuclear use but keep the construction going. If the talks run long, the number of launchers is the Soviet card, so only strengthen the camouflage
choices.why: The calculation that building up your hand even while negotiating is the basis of bargaining
choices.after: No. 76639 went out; the order to halt construction did not. The next morning an American low-level reconnaissance aircraft photographed launchers erected overnight, and the pictures lay on Kennedy’s desk beside your letter as he read it.

choices.text: Leave the nuclear use of the Lunas, the FKRs and the Il-28s to Pliyev’s decision in the event of a landing and a break in communications. Revive the September draft and send it by cable
choices.why: The judgment, putting the man on the spot first, that when the bombs fall, orders from Moscow come too late
choices.after: A different cable went out in place of No. 76639. Pliyev confirmed receipt, and the Luna battalion’s special warheads were moved up beside the launchers. At 5 p.m. Radio Moscow read your letter proposing the Turkey exchange. At that hour a U-2 was being tracked over Cuba.

choices.text: Categorically reconfirm the ban on nuclear use. Halt work on the R-12 and R-14 sites, allow only camouflage work at night, and send the Aleksandrovsk home
choices.why: The judgment that at the hour your words go out over the radio, the hands on the ground must be empty
choices.after: Three cables went out at 4:30 p.m.: the categorical confirmation of the ban on nuclear use; an order to stop all construction, since it was provoking the UN, and to camouflage only at night; and an order sending the Aleksandrovsk home with the Bratsk. Thirty minutes later the radio read the letter. At that hour a U-2 was being tracked over Cuba.

note.text: No. 76639, the cable halting construction and the cable recalling the Aleksandrovsk are in English translation as Wilson Center 117326, 117325 and 117327, with a Russian scan (No. 20076) at the National Security Archive. No published text of Pliyev’s No. 8/154 could be found anywhere, so it is given here only as the gist from secondary sources; it is an unverified item in the Phase 1 report. That the air-defense radars were authorized to operate from 26 October, and the movement of the warheads, are in the Statsenko division report.
note.src: WC/UMD 117326; WC/UMD 117325; WC/UMD 117327; WC/UMD 300465; Phase 1 issue 17

NK-H4.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, Presidium meeting room
NK-H4.title: Discretion
NK-H4.event: After the U-2 fell on 27 October, Kennedy waited no longer. Before dawn on 29 October (Havana) the US Air Force bombed the anti-aircraft missile sites and launch areas in Cuba, and Pliyev reported the loss of most of the R-12s and half the S-75 sites. A landing fleet has appeared off the coast west of Havana. Pliyev holds the discretion you gave him, and the Luna battalion’s special warheads are beside the launchers.
NK-H4.scene: Malinovsky stands beside the telephone in the meeting room. Communications with Havana keep breaking and coming back, and Pliyev’s last report was that once a landing begins he will respond at his discretion. You still have time to send one cable. Revoke the discretion and broadcast to Kennedy that you accept immediate withdrawal, and even if the landing is not stopped, no nuclear weapon is used. Leave the discretion in place and the landing force meets the Lunas on the beaches, and what the Americans answer with after that no one knows. Kozlov speaks of raising the alert of the Strategic Rocket Forces and ordering a retaliatory strike. Mikoyan tells you to think of the first bomb to fall on Soviet soil.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: Communications may be down for hours. If we are to send a revocation, it must go in this transmission. By the next one the landing may have begun.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: If one Luna falls on an American landing force, the Americans will answer not Cuba but the Soviet Union. What we sent to defend Cuba must not come back as the sacrifice of Soviet cities.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: The Americans bombed first. If we take back the discretion while Soviet soldiers are dying, Pliyev’s men meet the landing force bare-handed. The Strategic Rocket Forces must go on alert too, or the Americans will not stop.

choices.text: Keep the discretion. If they land, strike the landing force with Lunas but forbid strategic means, then immediately propose a ceasefire
choices.why: The calculation that tactical nuclear weapons can stop the landing and that it can end there
choices.after: Before dawn on 30 October, as the landing force closed on the shore, two Lunas burst over the sea. What followed is told in the Ending.

choices.text: Revoke the discretion at once and broadcast to Kennedy that you accept withdrawal. Even if the landing cannot be stopped, see that no nuclear weapon is used
choices.why: The judgment that losing Cuba and losing the world are two different things
choices.after: The revocation went out in the transmission, and Pliyev confirmed receipt. An hour later Radio Moscow read your acceptance of withdrawal. The landing did not stop, but no nuclear weapon was used. What followed is told in the Ending.

choices.text: Raise the alert of the Strategic Rocket Forces and order a retaliatory strike if the attacks continue, to make the Americans halt the landing
choices.why: The belief that only the missiles on Soviet soil can stop the Americans
choices.after: The order went out, and within hours American radar read the change on Soviet territory. What followed is told in the Ending.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact the order of 22 October and No. 76639 of 27 October forbade nuclear use, and there was no American air strike. The Phase 1 report’s Ending logic G drew the material for this path from the draft of 8 September, Khrushchev’s remarks of 22 October, the movement of warheads on 26–27 October and Castro’s letter of 26 October.
note.src: Phase 1 ending logic G; Phase 1 issue 1; WC/UMD 300465

NK-11.time: 10:45 a.m. (3:45 a.m. in Washington, 2:45 a.m. in Havana)
NK-11.place: Novo-Ogaryovo dacha outside Moscow, meeting room
NK-11.title: Novo-Ogaryovo
NK-11.clock: Less than a day until the deadline Robert Kennedy demanded for a reply (“by tomorrow”)

telegram.from: Defense Minister Malinovsky (certified by Ivanov, chief of the Main Operations Directorate, General Staff)
telegram.subject: American reconnaissance aircraft over Cuba, 27 October
telegram.text: At 1820 Moscow time on the 27th, to prevent the Americans from obtaining photographs, the 507th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment shot down the aircraft at an altitude of 21,000 meters with two surface-to-air missiles. The aircraft fell near Antilla. / US aircraft violated Cuban airspace eight times that day.

NK-11.event: Three things came in overnight. Alekseev’s cable: Castro considers intervention almost inevitable within 24 to 72 hours. Malinovsky’s report: Soviet forces in Cuba shot down a U-2 yesterday. Kennedy’s letter of 27 October: if the missiles are removed under UN supervision, the blockade will be lifted and Cuba will not be invaded. There is also a cable from Dobrynin. Robert Kennedy came to the embassy last night, demanded an answer by tomorrow, and said the missiles in Turkey would be gone within four to five months.
NK-11.scene: Sunday morning. You have called the Presidium not to the Kremlin but to the dacha at Novo-Ogaryovo. Birches stand outside the window, and the night’s cables lie on the table. A missile unit shot down a U-2 without orders from Moscow. Firing without orders is the first shot from the Soviet side; Castro says the invasion is two days away; and the long letter he sent last night asks how the Soviet Union should answer if the invasion comes. You read it as a proposal for a preemptive nuclear strike, and the thought will not leave you. Kennedy’s letter accepts almost exactly the offer as it stood yesterday, before Turkey was added. You tell the Presidium two things. If an attack is provoked, the order for a retaliatory strike has already been given. And you agree to dismantle the missile sites. Troyanovsky, beside the telephone, reports a rumor that another speech is coming soon from Washington. Malinovsky says it is still unknown whose decision the shoot-down was.

voices.who: Nikita Khrushchev (your words as recorded in Malin’s notes)
voices.text: 1. If an attack is provoked, the order has been given to deliver a retaliatory strike. 2. We agree to dismantle the missile sites.

voices.who: Aleksandr Alekseev (ambassador to Cuba, by cable)
voices.text: Castro considers intervention almost inevitable and expects it within roughly 24 to 72 hours.

voices.who: Anatoly Dobrynin (ambassador to the United States, gist of his cable)
voices.text: Robert Kennedy asked last night for an answer by tomorrow. The pressure from the military is heavy and the President cannot hold out long. He said the missiles in Turkey would be gone within four to five months, but that this could not be made a public condition.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: The shoot-down was reported as a decision to keep the photographs from being handed over, but we do not yet know whether Pliyev himself made it. The Americans will read this as the first Soviet shot.

voices.who: Oleg Troyanovsky (aide)
voices.text: There is talk of another presidential speech in Washington today. Moscow’s answer must go out on the radio before that speech. If it goes through translation and cipher, it will be too late.

choices.text: Hold the answer and keep the order for a retaliatory strike in the event of attack. First get Pliyev’s report on how the shoot-down happened
choices.why: A soldier’s caution: you cannot answer while you do not know the state of a unit that fired without orders
choices.after: No answer went out that day. Washington waited for Radio Moscow into the afternoon, and at the evening meeting the air-strike timetable came up again. Pliyev’s account did not arrive until night.

choices.text: Accept Kennedy’s letter of 27 October. Dictate a letter saying you have ordered the weapons dismantled, crated and returned, and broadcast it on the radio at 5 p.m.
choices.why: The judgment that on a day when a unit has fired without orders, you cannot draw things out another day
choices.after: You dictated the letter. In addition to the order to stop construction, the Soviet government had given a new order to dismantle the weapons you described as offensive, crate them and return them to the Soviet Union; and an American reconnaissance aircraft had entered the airspace over Chukotka this morning: what if it had been taken for a nuclear bomber? Radio Moscow would read the letter in English at 5 p.m., and the Russian original would be delivered to the embassy at 5:10. You also dictated cables to Castro and Alekseev.

choices.text: Hold to yesterday’s Turkey condition. Put off the answer until Kennedy accepts the withdrawal from Turkey as a public condition
choices.why: A gambler’s calculation: hold out one more day and the Americans will accept it publicly
choices.after: Gromyko wrote a short reply demanding Turkey again, and Dobrynin passed it to Robert Kennedy. The answer came that night: a public condition could not be accepted, and there was almost no time left.

note.text: Malin’s notes on the 28 October meeting (Protocol No. 63) record your two sentences, the dictation of the letter, and the dictation of cables to Castro and Alekseev. Dobrynin’s cable of 27 October (the meeting with RFK) is printed in CWIHP Bulletin 5, pp. 79–80 (Turkey “in four to five months,” an answer requested “by tomorrow (Sunday),” no public deal). Whether that cable was read before the decision is the fifth issue in the Phase 1 report. On 4 November Mikoyan explained to Castro that a “reliable report” on the morning of 28 October about preparations for an attack had prompted the decision. The rumor of a speech that Troyanovsky passed on rests on his memoirs, a secondary source. The widely quoted remark that “to save the world we must retreat” is not in Malin’s notes and is not used here.

pressure.title: The Day They Fired Without Orders
pressure.text: According to the overnight reports before you at Novo-Ogaryovo on Sunday morning, Soviet forces in Cuba shot down a U-2 without orders from Moscow, and Malinovsky’s report says only that it was done to keep the photographs out of American hands, so you still do not know who decided. Castro says the invasion is 24 to 72 hours away, and you read the letter he wrote through the night as a proposal that the Soviet Union strike first with nuclear weapons if the invasion comes. In Hungary in 1956 and Berlin in 1961 you could set the ending yourself, but this morning the forces in Cuba and Castro are moving ahead of you. You said only two sentences to the Presidium: if an attack is provoked, the order for a retaliatory strike has already been given; and you agree to dismantle the missile sites. Whether Dobrynin’s cable was read before the decision cannot be settled from the layout of the protocol alone, and Mikoyan later explained to Castro that a reliable report that morning about preparations for an attack had been the trigger.
