NK-H5.time: Morning (night of the 28th in Washington and Havana)
NK-H5.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, Presidium meeting room
NK-H5.title: A Public Exchange
NK-H5.clock: A few hours until the next ExComm meeting in Washington
NK-H5.event: Kennedy has replied that he cannot accept Turkey as a public condition. The NATO Council met through the night in Paris, and the Turkish government has declared its opposition to bargaining away the missiles on its soil to the Soviet Union. In London, Macmillan has publicly used the phrase “a dishonorable deal at the expense of an ally.” The US Air Force continues low-level reconnaissance over Cuba, and the landing force in Florida has finished embarking.
NK-H5.scene: The air in the meeting room is different from yesterday. You demanded Turkey publicly, and Kennedy refused publicly. Gromyko says what the Americans refused was not the condition but the publicity: the same thing in secret, they will accept. Kozlov says that if you hold out one more day, the Americans will give up Turkey in front of their allies. Mikoyan says that within that day the Americans may choose to bomb. Troyanovsky reports that U Thant in New York has proposed that the UN could arrange a timetable for the simultaneous withdrawal of both countries’ missiles.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister)
voices.text: The Americans did not refuse the condition; they refused the publicity. Accept yesterday’s letter and turn Turkey into a secret understanding, and we have the same thing in hand. A day late, but they will still take it.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: That NATO met through the night means the Americans are wavering. Hold out one more day and Kennedy will give up Turkey in front of his allies. This must end as a public Soviet victory.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: A day is time enough to decide on bombing. The U-2 fell yesterday and the American military has its pretext. We can have a public victory or the launchers in Cuba, not both.

choices.text: A day late, accept Kennedy’s letter of 27 October and turn Turkey into a secret understanding. Announce the withdrawal on the radio
choices.why: The calculation that if the problem was the publicity and not the condition, you simply drop the publicity
choices.after: The letter went out over Radio Moscow that afternoon. The acceptance was a day late, and for that day Washington had kept the air-strike timetable on the desk. Turkey remained only as words between Dobrynin and Robert Kennedy.

choices.text: Hold to a public exchange. A wavering NATO is the Americans’ problem; the Soviet Union trades like for like before the world
choices.why: The calculation that without a public victory there is nothing to lay before the Presidium
choices.after: Several more days passed. How it ended is told in the Ending. Whether the Americans accepted a public exchange over their allies’ objections, or chose to bomb, depended on what happened in the skies over Cuba during those days.

choices.text: Have U Thant broker a timetable at the UN for the simultaneous withdrawal from Cuba and Turkey. Make the exchange public, but in the UN’s name
choices.why: The calculation that if you borrow the UN’s name, the Americans too can save face and accept
choices.after: U Thant proposed a timetable for simultaneous withdrawal to both governments, and the Americans accepted on condition of consultation with NATO. The public exchange took the form of a UN document, and what followed is told in the Ending.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact you accepted Kennedy’s letter of 27 October on the morning of 28 October, and Turkey survived only in a secret letter dated 28 October. A public exchange was in fact considered, in your letter of 27 October and in the ExComm discussions in Washington; Macmillan’s phrase about a “dishonorable deal” is a recollection from his speech in the House of Commons on 30 October.
note.src: Phase 1 ending logic D; FRUS VI d66; FRUS VI d70

NK-H8.time: 11 p.m. (4 p.m. in Washington, 3 p.m. in Havana)
NK-H8.place: Novo-Ogaryovo dacha outside Moscow, meeting room
NK-H8.title: The Retaliation Order
NK-H8.clock: About seven hours until dawn in Havana (the earliest hour for an American air strike)
NK-H8.event: Moscow’s answer did not go out all day. The evening meeting in Washington put the air-strike timetable back on the table, and a report has come through KGB channels that Kennedy has signed the order for an air strike before dawn on Monday. Pliyev’s account arrived at night. The shoot-down was decided by his deputies Grechko and Garbuz while he was ill, to keep the photographs from getting through. Pliyev writes that if an air strike comes he will use every means of air defense, and that he awaits Moscow’s orders.
NK-H8.scene: Night at the dacha. You have spent a day and gained only the story of the shoot-down. Malinovsky says seven hours remain until dawn in Havana, and one cable can be sent in that time. Broadcast to Kennedy that you accept withdrawal, and the air strike can be stopped. Leave the retaliatory strike order in place, and when the strike begins the R-12s in Cuba will fire, and that is war on Soviet soil. Kozlov proposes releasing only the tactical means to strike the landing force and forbidding strategic means. Mikoyan proposes putting out the broadcast within the hour. Troyanovsky has the Radio Moscow announcer standing by.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: Seven hours until dawn in Havana. If the retaliation order stands, Statsenko fires as ordered when the first bomb falls. After that, even I cannot stop it.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: If the broadcast goes out within the hour, Kennedy can cancel the strike. We are only accepting tonight what we could have accepted yesterday. We can pay the price of a day, but not the price of the world.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: Forbid strategic means, but release the Lunas. If the landing force is stopped on the beaches, the Americans will not strike Soviet territory; they will come to the table. We cannot leave Pliyev empty-handed to take the bombing.

choices.text: Forbid strategic means and let Pliyev strike only the landing force with Lunas. Take the air strike, but stop the landing on the beaches
choices.why: The calculation to release only the weapons that can end it inside Cuba
choices.after: The cable went out in the transmission. The air strike began at dawn, and Pliyev waited for the landing fleet with the discretion in his hands.

choices.text: Broadcast to Kennedy at once that you accept withdrawal, and cancel the retaliation order. A day late, but it gets in before the air strike
choices.why: The judgment that you can pay the price of a day, but not the price of the world
choices.after: Radio Moscow read the acceptance at midnight (4 p.m. in Washington). Whether Washington canceled the strike, or could not recall aircraft already in the air, is told in the Ending.

choices.text: Leave the retaliation order in place. If the Americans bomb, the R-12s in Cuba answer, and the Soviet Union tells the world it did not fire first
choices.why: The belief that when the side struck first fires back, it is retaliation, not aggression
choices.after: The order stood. At dawn in Havana the first bomb fell, and what followed is told in the Ending.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact you decided on the morning of 28 October and broadcast at 5 p.m. That Grechko and Garbuz decided the shoot-down in Pliyev’s absence is Garbuz’s recollection from 1992; Malinovsky’s report names no decision-maker. The words “if an attack is provoked, a retaliatory strike” are in Malin’s notes for 28 October.
note.src: Malin 10/28; Garbuz 1992; Phase 1 issue 2

NK-12.time: 4 p.m. (9 a.m. in Washington, 8 a.m. in Havana)
NK-12.place: Novo-Ogaryovo dacha outside Moscow, Defense Ministry liaison room
NK-12.title: Too Hasty
NK-12.clock: One hour until the radio broadcast (5 p.m.)

telegram.text: We consider that you were too hasty in shooting down the American U-2 reconnaissance aircraft, at a time when an agreement to avert an attack on Cuba by peaceful means was taking shape. / The Soviet government has decided to dismantle the R-12s and remove them. Begin carrying out this measure. / Confirm receipt.

NK-12.event: The letter has been translated and is in the hands of a Radio Moscow announcer. In one hour it will be read in English; ten minutes after that the Russian original goes to the American embassy. Before then you must settle the cable to Pliyev. If the unit that brought down a U-2 yesterday without orders fires again today, the letter is worthless. Who decided on the shootdown has still not been reported to Moscow.
NK-12.scene: Malinovsky has come in with drafts of two cables. One is No. 76645, warning that the shootdown was too hasty and announcing the decision to dismantle; the other is No. 4/835, which bans the use of the S-75 and, to avoid clashes with American reconnaissance aircraft, bans fighter sorties as well. Kozlov says the commander who fired without orders must be replaced. Mikoyan says that if Pliyev is replaced, Castro will treat the shootdown as his own cause and fire more. You yourself are half inclined to think the shootdown did some good in the end, since it frightened the Americans. But today is not the day to say so.

voices.who: Rodion Malinovsky (defense minister)
voices.text: We still do not know whether Pliyev fired or his deputy did. The first thing is to make sure nobody fires again. Responsibility can be settled once they are home.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: Leave in place a commander who brought down an American aircraft without orders from Moscow, and the next commander will do the same. Recall Pliyev and hand command to the chief of staff.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: Change the commander today and Havana will read it as the Soviet Union punishing its own general in front of the Americans. Castro will take it as an insult and fire more anti-aircraft guns. A warning is the right place to stop.

choices.text: Send Pliyev only the warning that he was “too hasty,” and ban the S-75 and fighter sorties. Transmit the dismantling order with it
choices.why: Stopping any further firing comes first; responsibility can be settled later
choices.after: No. 76645 went out at 4 p.m., No. 4/835 at 6:30 p.m. Garbuz later recalled that “the commander in chief did not criticize us.” At 5 p.m. Radio Moscow read the letter. In Havana, Castro learned of the decision from that broadcast.

choices.text: Dismiss Pliyev and recall Grechko. Fix responsibility for the shootdown clearly, so that there is something to tell the Americans
choices.why: Firing without orders must be punished at once, or there will be a next time
choices.after: The dismissal cable went out, and Pliyev confirmed receipt. In Havana, Castro heard the news from Alekseev and said the Soviet Union had punished its own general in front of the Americans. Cuban anti-aircraft guns fired on low-flying aircraft again that evening.

choices.text: Endorse the shootdown, without reproach, as an authorized act of air defense and send only the dismantling order. The Americans were frightened partly because of it
choices.why: If the result was good, there is no reason to scold the men on the spot
choices.after: Only the dismantling order went out. Pliyev’s air defense units kept their radars on, and when American reconnaissance aircraft came back over Cuba the next day, Moscow had to wait beside the telephone.

note.text: English translations of Nos. 76645 and 4/835 are at Wilson Center 117329 and 117330. Who decided on the shootdown is the second issue in the Phase 1 report. Garbuz recalled in 1992 that he and Grechko had decided while Pliyev was ill; Malinovsky’s report of 28 October names no decision-maker, and the rebuke went to Pliyev. You called the shootdown “a useful act in the end” in your letter to Castro of 30 October.
note.src: WC/UMD 117329; WC/UMD 117330; Garbuz 1992; Phase 1 issue 2; PBS 10/30

NK-13.time: 5:10 p.m. (9:10 a.m. in Washington, 9:10 a.m. in Havana)
NK-13.place: Novo-Ogaryovo dacha outside Moscow, conference room
NK-13.title: Restraint, and More Restraint

telegram.to: F. Castro, Prime Minister of the Republic of Cuba
telegram.subject: (no subject)
telegram.text: I would like to advise you, at this critical moment, not to be carried away by emotion and to show restraint. / Yesterday you shot down one of these aircraft, though before this you never shot them down when they flew over Cuban territory. The aggressors will use such a step for their own ends. / Show patience, restraint, and more restraint.

NK-13.event: Radio Moscow read the letter in English ten minutes ago. The Russian original is now going into the American embassy. In Havana the broadcast has been on the radio since 9 a.m., and Castro will learn of the decision from it before he hears from you. Your cable to him has not yet left. His letter of 26 October, written through the night, is in, and you have read it as a proposal that if an invasion comes the Soviet Union should strike first with nuclear weapons. Castro will later explain that he meant no such thing; he was speaking of the case of an invasion.
NK-13.scene: The conference room is quiet after the broadcast. You dictate the letter to Castro. You must say that there was no time to tell him before the decision, that you have secured an American pledge not to invade, and something about the aircraft shot down yesterday: that he fired on aircraft he had not fired on until yesterday, and the aggressors will make use of it. Mikoyan says the trouble is that Castro will receive this letter after he has heard the radio. Gromyko says Alekseev must be told to give a positive answer on U Thant’s visit to Havana and on access to the launch sites. Kozlov says the demand in Castro’s letter must be refuted publicly, so the world knows the Soviet Union refused nuclear war.

voices.who: Aleksandr Alekseev (ambassador in Havana, gist of his cable of the evening of 27 October)
voices.text: Castro and Dorticós said yesterday’s Turkey letter was “written with great diplomatic skill,” but that some officers and some of the public are confused. To the request that they publicly announce a ban on work on the special weapons, they said they would make Guantánamo a reciprocal condition.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: Castro hears it on the radio first and gets the letter afterward. That gap will stay as a grievance between Cuba and the Soviet Union. The letter should explain at length and reproach briefly.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister)
voices.text: Alekseev needs instructions. If U Thant offers to come to Havana, accept, and have him answer positively on access to the launch sites too. If Castro refuses inspection, the Americans will put off their pledge not to invade.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: Castro’s letter asked the Soviet Union to start a nuclear war. The world must know that the Soviet Union refused. The Soviet people knowing matters more than that man’s feelings.

choices.text: Leave the shootdown out and explain only how the decision came about. Do not ask the Cuban army to stop its anti-aircraft fire; put off the question of inspection
choices.why: Saving an ally’s face lasts longer than one burst of gunfire
choices.after: The letter went out with the explanation alone. In his reply that evening Castro explained of his own accord how he had brought 50 anti-aircraft batteries into action, and wrote that he would hold fire only while the negotiations went on. Inspection, he said, he opposed in principle.

choices.text: Send Castro a letter urging restraint. Raise the shootdown and tell him not to fire again, and propose that U Thant’s visit settle the inspection question
choices.why: Soothe the ally, but stop any further firing, or the deal dies
choices.after: The letter went to Alekseev by cable. Castro heard the radio first and received the letter afterward, and later said he had felt not relief but deep anger. That evening he announced his five points, and in his reply to you wrote that he would hold his anti-aircraft fire only while the negotiations went on, and that he opposed inspection in principle.

choices.text: Refute the demand in Castro’s letter publicly, and order Pliyev to restrict Cuban troops’ access to Soviet positions
choices.why: Showing the world that you refused nuclear war matters more than the ally
choices.after: TASS issued a statement that the Soviet Union rejected any proposal for a preemptive nuclear strike, and Havana saw at once that it was aimed at them. Castro would not see Alekseev for three days, and Cuban anti-aircraft guns went on firing at low-flying aircraft.

note.text: The letter to Castro of 28 October exists in two translations, at Wilson Center 114504 (Savranskaya translation) and in the National Security Archive document set. In one, the last sentence reads “patience, restraint, and more restraint”; in the other, “patience, firmness, and more firmness.” Castro’s letter of 26 October is the fourth issue in the Phase 1 report: you read it as a proposal for a preemptive nuclear strike, and Castro explained that he was speaking of the case of an invasion. The text gives that passage only in gist. The broadcast went out at 1700 Moscow time, which was 9 a.m. in Havana and Washington (standard time resumed on 28 October); the hour at which Castro heard it (“around noon”) and the gap before the letter arrived rest on secondary sources drawn from Cuban recollections, so the text gives no time. Castro’s reply of 28 October (50 anti-aircraft batteries, a halt to firing during negotiations, opposition to inspection in principle) is in the National Security Archive document set.
note.src: WC/UMD 90509; NSA CMC 19621028khrlet; Phase 1 issue 4; Phase 1 issue 12; Castro 10/28 (NSA 19621028caslet)

NK-14.time: Night (afternoon in Washington, afternoon in Havana)
NK-14.place: Novo-Ogaryovo dacha outside Moscow, resumed session (small group)
NK-14.title: The Secret Letter

telegram.subject: For transmission to R. Kennedy
telegram.text: Contact R. Kennedy immediately and convey the following. / The ideas R. Kennedy set out on the President’s instructions are meeting with understanding in Moscow. / Today a reply to the President’s letter of 27 October will go out by radio, and that reply will be the most favorable one.

NK-14.event: Gromyko’s instruction reached Washington an hour and a half after the broadcast. Dobrynin saw Robert Kennedy all the same, and reported that he called it “a great relief” and said that today, at last, he would get to see his children. The missiles in Turkey would be gone within four to five months, but that had to be kept strictly secret, and nothing could be exchanged in writing. In the evening Kennedy issued a statement welcoming your decision as “statesmanlike.”
NK-14.scene: A small meeting, without Gromyko or Malinovsky. You read Dobrynin’s report and the KGB cables. The missiles in Turkey have been promised only by word of mouth. Mikoyan says the deal survives only if the secret is kept. The opinion Gromyko left behind is that there must be a document, or the Americans will deny it later. Kozlov says the Presidium needs proof of victory, so you should demand that Turkey go into a public statement. Other decisions are piling up: that U Thant can be shown the dismantling; that the Red Cross should inspect ships at sea; a cable asking Castro to agree to Red Cross entry; and an information letter for Kennedy. You have decided to send Deputy Foreign Minister Kuznetsov to New York.

voices.who: Anatoly Dobrynin (ambassador in Washington, cable)
voices.text: Robert Kennedy said, “This is a great relief.” “Today, at last, I will get to see my children.”

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: Turkey must stay secret. Kennedy can keep his word only if he can deny it in front of his allies. One secret letter is enough. Make it public and you lose the missiles and the promise both.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister, opinion left behind)
voices.text: In four months nobody will remember a spoken promise. It is enough to hand Robert Kennedy a letter and leave on record only that the Americans received it. No publicity is needed, but a document is.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: The Presidium will ask why the missiles were withdrawn. A pledge not to invade Cuba is not enough. Turkey must go in publicly, so that this becomes an exchange and not a retreat.

choices.text: Stop at Dobrynin’s oral understanding, with no document. Watch whether the Americans take the missiles out of Turkey within four to five months, and judge then
choices.why: Leaving the other side all its face is the way to make it keep its word
choices.after: No letter was written. The missiles in Turkey quietly disappeared the following April, but the Soviet Union had no document with which to say it had been a bargain. In the Presidium the question of why the missiles had been withdrawn lingered all winter.

choices.text: Demand that the Americans put the Turkish withdrawal in a public statement. You need proof to lay before the Presidium as a victory
choices.why: To turn a decision that looks like retreat into an exchange, it has to be public
choices.after: Dobrynin conveyed the demand, and Robert Kennedy refused on the spot: make it public and there is no deal. The Americans never mentioned Turkey again, and the Soviet Union could no longer speak of it publicly either.

choices.text: Record the Turkey understanding in a secret letter. Write that the discussion will continue confidentially through Robert Kennedy and the Soviet ambassador
choices.why: Publicity kills the deal and a spoken word lets it be forgotten, so one document is needed
choices.after: A secret letter dated 28 October was drawn up, agreeing that discussion of this question would continue confidentially through Robert Kennedy and the Soviet ambassador. Dobrynin handed it to Robert Kennedy on the 29th; Robert Kennedy studied it overnight and on the 30th gave it back, saying it contained a quid pro quo. No record remained.

note.text: The decisions of the resumed session are in the Malin notes (continuation of Protocol No. 63). Gromyko’s instruction and Dobrynin’s report (“the instruction arrived 1.5 hours after the broadcast,” “a great relief,” Turkey to be kept secret) are printed in CWIHP Bulletin 5, p. 77, and Kennedy’s “statesmanlike” statement is the White House statement of 28 October. The text of the secret letter and the circumstances of its return are in FRUS VI d70 and its footnote; the two Phase 1 reports grade the account of the return differently, so this is an item to re-verify.
note.src: Malin 10/28; Gromyko 10/28 (Bulletin 5); Dobrynin 10/28 (Bulletin 5); FRUS VI d70; Phase 1 issue 14; Kennedy 10/28 statement

NK-15.time: Afternoon (morning in Washington, morning in Havana)
NK-15.place: The Kremlin, Moscow, office of the First Secretary
NK-15.title: A Remarkable Man

telegram.to: F. Castro, Prime Minister of the Republic of Cuba
telegram.subject: (no subject)
telegram.text: In your cable of 27 October you proposed that we be the first to deliver a nuclear strike against the enemy’s territory. You know where that would have led. It would not have been a simple strike but the start of a thermonuclear world war. / Dear Comrade Fidel Castro, I understand your reasons, but I consider the proposal wrong. / The shooting down of the American aircraft over Cuban territory passed without complications, and so in the end it was a useful act.

NK-15.event: The secret letter Dobrynin handed to Robert Kennedy yesterday has come back today. The Havana newspaper Revolución ran “Khrushchev Orders Withdrawal of Rockets” across its front page on the 29th, with Castro’s five points beneath it. Alekseev reports that the Cuban leadership is angry at having learned of the decision from the radio, and rejects inspection in any form. U Thant leaves for Havana tomorrow.
NK-15.scene: Before writing the letter you set down a note. Castro is a remarkable man. Yesterday he sent a proposal to start a nuclear war, and he did it out of despair. The Soviet Union has obtained from the Americans a statement that they will not invade. On that note you dictate a long letter: what Castro’s cable of 27 October meant, why the Soviet Union refused, what kind of victory the American pledge not to invade is. Mikoyan says that if the letter contains the words “proposed to strike first with nuclear weapons,” that is the only sentence Castro will remember. Gromyko says Kuznetsov arrives in New York today and someone must go to Havana as well. Mikoyan says he will go himself. Kozlov says a letter demanding that Castro accept UN inspection should come first: without inspection there is no American pledge not to invade.

voices.who: Nikita Khrushchev (your note of 30 October)
voices.text: Castro is a remarkable man. Yesterday he sent a proposal to start a nuclear war, and he did it because he was in despair. The Soviet Union has obtained from the Americans a statement that they will not invade.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (first deputy chairman of the Presidium)
voices.text: Nikita Sergeyevich, that man will forget every other sentence in the letter and remember the one: “proposed to strike first with nuclear weapons.” I will go to Havana. This is not something a document can do.

voices.who: Andrei Gromyko (foreign minister)
voices.text: Kuznetsov meets McCloy and Stevenson in New York today. The inspection question cannot be settled in New York, only in Havana. A member of the Presidium must go to Havana.

voices.who: Frol Kozlov (secretary of the Central Committee)
voices.text: If Castro refuses inspection, the Americans will put off their pledge not to invade and keep the blockade. A letter telling him to accept inspection comes before a letter of explanation. The Soviet Union is withdrawing Soviet missiles, and Cuba has no right to stand in the way.

choices.text: Send no letter, only Mikoyan, to explain in person. Put the shootdown and the first-strike proposal in writing and only the wound remains
choices.why: Words spoken by a man on the spot hurt less than words that stay on paper
choices.after: Mikoyan landed in Havana on 2 November. With no letter, Castro heard for the first time from Mikoyan’s own mouth why his proposal had been refused, and the two men argued for three weeks over inspection and the Il-28s.

choices.text: Send Castro a letter demanding that he accept UN inspection. Without inspection the American pledge not to invade will not stand
choices.why: To close the deal, you must ask a price of the ally too
choices.after: Castro received the letter and would not see Alekseev for three days. Inspection never took place; instead, the Americans counted the missiles on departing ships at sea. Mikoyan did not go to Havana until November.

choices.text: Explain the decision to Castro in a long letter, and send Mikoyan to Havana and Kuznetsov to New York
choices.why: The ally needs an explanation and the negotiation needs a man on the spot, or the deal is not finished
choices.after: Alekseev delivered the letter on the 31st. Castro was hurt most by the phrase “proposed to strike first with nuclear weapons,” and said either the translation was wrong or Khrushchev had misunderstood. Mikoyan landed in Havana on 2 November, and stayed on even after the news of his wife’s death reached him. It took three more weeks for the blockade to be lifted.

note.text: The letter of 30 October is the English translation from the appendix to Blight et al., Cuba on the Brink, as reprinted by PBS; your preliminary note is at Wilson Center 108406. The passage on a preemptive nuclear strike is given in gist rather than quoted at length. Alekseev’s cables of 31 October and 2 November record which phrase hurt Castro and an error in the Russian original that the embassy corrected in translation. The return of the secret letter follows the footnote to FRUS VI d70. The Kuznetsov–McCloy meeting of 30 October is in FRUS XI, and the death of Mikoyan’s wife is confirmed by a Czechoslovak embassy cable of 6 November (which gives no date). The front-page headline of Revolución of 29 October is a Cuban-side report based on Gilly’s account.

epilogues.A: On 20 November Kennedy announced the lifting of the blockade, and the same day Malinovsky ordered Pliyev to send back six nuclear bombs, twelve Luna warheads and eighty FKR warheads aboard the Atkarsk. Mikoyan, who argued with Castro for three more weeks over the Il-28s, left Havana at the end of November. On 3 December you summed up for the Presidium: to say that we retreated was malicious weakness; the Americans had frightened themselves, and had we held out a little longer, perhaps nothing would have happened. The Jupiters in Turkey quietly disappeared in April 1963, and in October 1964 the Presidium removed you from office. Meanwhile, at 9 a.m. on 28 October, Washington time, Radio Moscow’s English-language broadcast was coming into Kennedy’s room.
epilogues.B: American air strikes pounded the launch sites and the surface-to-air missile bases in Cuba for three days, and a landing followed. How many of the roughly 44,000 Soviet troops planned in Malinovsky’s memorandum came home was not known for a long time. No nuclear weapon was used, but it was the first war in which Soviet soldiers were killed by American troops, and the winter in Berlin passed under its shadow.
epilogues.C: It took the two capitals several hours to confirm where the first nuclear explosion had been, and the orders given in those hours decided the world that came after. What the order of 22 October and No. 76639 of 27 October forbade had happened in the field, and you learned of it from a broadcast.
epilogues.D: The United States accepted a public exchange over the objections of its NATO allies. The missiles in Turkey and in Cuba disappeared together on a timetable drawn up by the UN, and you could lay the word exchange before the Presidium. Within NATO, America’s word carried less weight; within the Soviet Union, your position lasted a little longer.
epilogues.E: U Thant’s two-week freeze became two months. Neutral observers watched the launch sites in Cuba, and the missiles stood where they were, as collateral for the negotiations. While blockade and freeze together outlasted the winter, the world began to forget Cuba, and in the spring of 1963 the missiles were withdrawn in the name of the UN.
epilogues.F: The blockade ran into the new year and the missiles stayed in Cuba. The United States could neither shoot nor lift it, and in the spring of 1963 you put those missiles on the table at the Berlin negotiations. What became of Berlin that spring is the story of the next crisis.
epilogues.G: Two Lunas burst over the sea off the landing beach, and the landing stopped. The United States did not strike Soviet territory, and the Soviet Union fired no more. After several weeks of negotiation every nuclear weapon left Cuba, but the world after a nuclear weapon had been used was not the world before. Whether Pliyev held a signed authorization was disputed for a long time afterward.
epilogues.H: The barrier at Helmstedt stayed down all winter, and an airlift flew into West Berlin once more. While the blockade in the Caribbean and the blockade of Berlin together ran into the new year, no first shot was fired at either, but the two crises remained entangled until the spring of 1963.

dossier.t: Born in April 1894 in Kalinovka, a village in Kursk province, he is 68 in October 1962. As a boy he moved with his family to Yuzovka in the Donbas, where he worked as a mechanic in the mines and factories, and in 1918 he joined the Bolsheviks. He is one of the few who ran the party organizations of Moscow and Ukraine under Stalin and survived, and during the war he was a political commissar on the Stalingrad front. After becoming first secretary in 1953, he delivered the secret speech denouncing Stalin’s crimes at the Twentieth Party Congress in February 1956, and that November he sent troops into Hungary. Since 1958 he has also been Chairman of the Council of Ministers, holding party and government in one hand. His speech is coarse, he loves proverbs and figures of speech, and he has a habit of leaving his text behind and speaking at length off the cuff. Back from Bulgaria in May 1962, you carry in your head a worry about the American missiles in Turkey, across the Black Sea.

With his wife Nina Petrovna he has Rada, Sergei and Elena; Leonid, his son by his first wife, was a fighter pilot who did not come back from the front in March 1943. His son Sergei is an engineer in a missile design bureau. The man he has worked with longest in the Presidium is Mikoyan, who is said to have questioned the deployment plan in May and who has long played the part of asking the second question when you charge ahead. Kozlov, the second secretary, is rough; Gromyko brings the Foreign Ministry’s drafts; Malinovsky, the defense minister, a soldier since Stalingrad days, is the man who buys time against your improvisations. Your aide Troyanovsky handles the telephone and the cables. Ambassador Dobrynin in Washington meets Robert Kennedy, and Ambassador Alekseev in Havana reports what Castro says by coded cable. Pliyev, the commander in Cuba, is a ground-forces general you picked over a rocket-forces officer for the sake of cover.

His greatest fears are losing Cuba and the strategic balance with the United States. At the Bay of Pigs in April 1961 the Americans failed once with a force of exiles; next time, you believe, they will send their own army. The imbalance weighed on you: American nuclear weapons, like the Jupiter missiles in Turkey, sit on the Soviet border, while Soviet missiles do not sit on America’s. The Kennedy you met in Vienna in June 1961 struck you as a young and unsteady opponent, and that August the Wall went up in Berlin. Relations with China were deteriorating. Your hope was to slip the missiles in, announce them together with a treaty once the American midterm elections were over in November, go to Cuba, and make it impossible for Kennedy to repeat what he did at the Bay of Pigs. What you wanted was not war but a threat that would make the United States take its hands off Cuba.

movers.intro: Why Khrushchev sent missiles to Cuba, and why he took them out on 28 October, remain disputed among historians even after the Soviet archives opened in the 1990s. The defense of Cuba, the strategic balance with the United States, Berlin and Turkey, and Khrushchev’s own character are each given different weight. The main views are these:
views: Aleksandr Fursenko and Timothy Naftali: the first to read the Soviet documents widely, they see the defense of Cuba as the first motive for the deployment, but regard it as a gamble aimed at the strategic balance and Berlin as well. The withdrawal decision of 28 October, they hold, was taken under the weight of that morning’s reports that an American attack was imminent, and it is unclear whether Dobrynin’s cable on Turkey was read before the decision.

William Taubman: in his biography he explains the Cuban decision through Khrushchev’s character. An inferiority complex about his lack of education as a former miner, a temperament that could not bear being looked down on, and an impulsiveness that sought to solve several problems with a single bold stroke combined, he argues, to put Khrushchev in a position he could not get out of by himself.

Michael Dobbs: following 27 October hour by hour, he stresses that neither leader controlled what was happening on the ground. The U-2 shot down without orders, B-59 beneath the sea and the tactical nuclear weapons inside Cuba pushed Khrushchev’s decision, and he hurried, Dobbs argues, because he knew war could begin not by order but by accident.

Vladislav Zubok: portrays Khrushchev as a leader who carried the ideals of the revolution and the interests of the empire in one body. The Cuban deployment grew out of his optimism, his faith in a tide of history that socialism was driving forward; the withdrawal cracked that faith, and the distrust within the leadership that ended in his removal in 1964 grew from here.
movers.note: Khrushchev’s own memoirs, and the recollections of Troyanovsky and Sergei Khrushchev, paint the decision of 28 October as a retreat to save the world, but no such words appear in Malin’s notes. At the Presidium on 3 December he said that to call it a retreat was malicious weakness, and added that had they held out a little longer, perhaps nothing would have happened.
